name: Books & Training
title: Arborist Books, Standards & Training Materials
meta: Arborist books and training materials for climbers and crew leaders: ANSI Z133 and A300 standards, ISA certification study guides and field references.
intro: Our arborist books and training materials cover the standards, study guides and field references that working tree crews actually lean on. Start with ANSI Z133 for safety and A300 for pruning practice, then build out from there.

guide.h: Why every crew needs a small library
p: Gear wears out and gets replaced. What a climber knows stays on the truck every day. A short shelf of good arborist books gives a crew a shared language for how work gets done: what a proper pruning cut looks like, what a safe drop zone is, how a rigging load really behaves when a piece comes off the stem.

Books also settle arguments. When two climbers disagree about a tie-in point or how to set a lowering line, the answer is usually already written down by people who have spent decades studying it. Keeping the current standards in the cab means the crew leader can point to the page instead of relying on whoever talks loudest.

Books matter for crew leaders and business owners too. Bidding municipal work, writing a pruning spec or answering a client who asks why you will not top their tree all go better when you can cite the standard and the reasoning behind it.

guide.h: The standards: ANSI Z133 and ANSI A300
p: ANSI Z133 is the American safety standard for arboricultural operations. It covers climbing systems, connectors, rigging, chainsaw use, electrical hazards, aerial lifts and traffic control. If you climb or run a crew in the US, it is the baseline your gear and procedures are measured against, and it is updated periodically, so make sure the copy you train from is current.

ANSI A300 is the tree care performance standard. Where Z133 is about keeping people safe, A300 is about doing right by the tree: pruning objectives, cut placement, support systems, lightning protection and more. Many municipal and utility contracts reference A300 directly, so knowing it is part of winning and keeping that work.

The ISA Certified Arborist Study Guide is the standard prep text for the Certified Arborist exam. It covers tree biology, soils, identification, pruning, diagnosis, safety and more, and it stays useful long after the test as a desk reference for the parts of the job that are not climbing.

For climbing technique, The Tree Climber's Companion by Jeff Jepson is a classic pocket guide that a lot of climbers started with, and it is often the book people mean when they ask for arborist books for beginners. Pair a field guide like that with hands-on training from a qualified instructor. No book replaces time on the rope under someone who can watch your system and correct it.
Rigging and tree risk assessment each have their own references as you move up. Add them when the work calls for it rather than buying a whole shelf at once.

guide.h: How to use books on a real crew
p: Pick one topic a week for the tailgate meeting and read a page or two out loud: tie-in points, drop zone communication, chipper safety. Keep the standards in a dry bag in the truck so they do not turn into pulp. When a new climber joins, hand them the study guide and the climbing reference before you hand them a saddle.
Remember that books explain the why, while manufacturer instructions govern each specific device. Read both, follow both, and inspect life-support gear before every climb.

faq.q: What are the best arborist books for a new climber?
faq.a: Start with the current ANSI Z133 safety standard, a climbing field guide such as The Tree Climber's Companion, and the ISA Certified Arborist Study Guide once you are ready to learn the wider science of tree care.

faq.q: Is the ANSI Z133 standard required reading?
faq.a: If you work on trees in the US, Z133 is the safety standard employers, insurers and inspectors refer to. Every climber and crew leader should know what it says about their gear and tasks.

faq.q: What is the difference between Z133 and A300?
faq.a: Z133 is about worker safety during tree work. A300 is about tree care practice, such as how and why to prune. Most professional crews keep both on hand.

faq.q: Can I learn to climb trees from a book?
faq.a: A book is a good foundation, but climbing should be learned with hands-on training from a qualified instructor. Use books to reinforce what you practice, not to replace supervision.

name: Climbing
title: Climbing Tree Gear: Saddles, Spurs, Rope Tools & More
meta: Climbing tree gear for working arborists: saddles, spurs, carabiners, friction devices, lanyards, helmets and throw line, explained by tree people.
intro: This is the hub for all of our climbing tree gear: saddles, spurs, hardware, friction devices, lanyards, helmets and throw line. Whether you are building a first kit or replacing worn tree gear, the sections below get you to the right shelf fast.

guide.h: How the climbing department is organized
p: Climbing gear breaks down by the job each piece does in your system. Saddles and harnesses are what you sit in. Rope tools, friction devices and hitch cord control how you move. Carabiners, rings, swivels and pulleys connect it all together. Lanyards and fliplines keep you positioned while you cut, and spurs get you up spars and removals.

Around that core sit the support items: helmets, throw weights and line for setting your tie-in, and gear bags for keeping it clean. Each subcategory has its own buying guide, so you can drill down to exactly what you need.

If you are not sure where something lives, start with the climbing gear section. It holds most of the hardware and devices, from ascenders to carabiners, and each listing explains what the item does in a working system.

A working kit starts with a saddle that fits, a climbing rope rated for arborist use, a friction hitch or mechanical device, connectors that meet ANSI Z133, a flipline or adjustable lanyard, a helmet and a throw line setup. Buy the saddle first and fit it in person if you can, because comfort decides how long you will stay productive in the tree.

If you are just starting, a moving rope system (MRS) with a hitch and micro pulley is simple to learn and inspect. Many climbers later add a stationary rope system (SRS) for long ascents and big canopies. Either way, get trained before you leave the ground.

Do not overlook the small items that make a kit usable on day one: a micro pulley to tend your hitch, a friction saver to protect your rope and the tree, a rope bag to keep the line clean, and a couple of gear carabiners for tools. A complete tree climbing kit is often the easiest way to get all of that matched and compatible in one go.

We get asked about used tree climbing gear a lot. Hardware such as carabiners and pulleys can be inspected, but you rarely know how textile gear like rope, saddles and lanyards has been stored, loaded or exposed to chemicals. For life-support items, buy new from a source you trust and keep a record of when each item went into service.
Crews outfitting several climbers can save by standardizing on one or two connector models and one rope diameter. That keeps spares interchangeable and makes daily inspections faster.

Every piece of life-support tree gear should meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions, and be inspected before each climb. Retire anything that has been shock loaded, cut, glazed, cracked or that you simply cannot vouch for. When in doubt, take it out of service.

Treat inspection as part of the climb, not a separate chore. Run your rope through your hands as you flake it out, check every connector gate as you clip it to your saddle, and look at stitching on your bridge and lanyard before you leave the ground. Keep a simple log for each climber's life-support gear with dates in service and any notes from inspections. When a crew shares gear, the log is how everyone knows what has happened to it.
Finally, pair good gear with good habits: a work plan, a clear drop zone, a trained ground person and an aerial rescue plan for every climb.

faq.q: What tree gear do I need to start climbing?
faq.a: At minimum: a fitted arborist saddle, an arborist climbing rope, a friction hitch or mechanical friction device, Z133-compliant locking connectors, a lanyard or flipline, a helmet and a throw line kit, plus proper training.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy used climbing gear?
faq.a: Used metal hardware can sometimes be inspected and trusted, but used rope, saddles and lanyards are hard to evaluate. For life-support textiles, buying new is the safer choice.

faq.q: What is the difference between MRS and SRS?
faq.a: In a moving rope system the rope runs over the anchor and moves as you climb. In a stationary rope system the rope is fixed and you move along it with a device. Both are common in tree work.

faq.q: Do I need spurs to climb trees?
faq.a: Only for removals and some spar work. Spurs wound living trees, so they are not used for pruning trees that are staying, except in a rescue.

name: Climbing Gear
h1: Tree Climbing Gear & Arborist Climbing Equipment
title: Tree Climbing Gear & Arborist Climbing Equipment
meta: Tree climbing gear for arborists: ascenders, friction devices, carabiners, lanyards, pulleys, friction savers and rope bags. Practical buying advice.
intro: Shop tree climbing gear built for real arborist work: ascenders, mechanical friction devices, carabiners, lanyards, pulleys, friction savers and storage. This is the arborist climbing equipment that sits between your saddle and your rope.

p: Your saddle and rope get most of the attention, but the small parts decide how smooth your day goes. This section holds the tree climbing equipment that connects and controls your system: ascenders and foot loops, mechanical friction devices for MRS and SRS, hitch cord and split tails, micro pulleys, swivels, rings, carabiners, snap hooks, lanyards and fliplines, chainsaw lanyards and friction savers.

Most of it is life-support gear, which means it should meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's rating for the way you plan to use it. Read the instructions that come with each device. Many are approved only for specific rope diameters and constructions.

If you are not sure which subcategory fits, think about where the item sits in your system. Anything between your saddle and the rope is usually here; the saddle itself, spurs, helmets and throw line have their own departments.

guide.h: Matching gear to your climbing system
p: Start with your rope diameter and system. An 11.7 mm rope and a mechanical device rated for 11 to 13 mm will not behave like a hitch tied on a 13 mm rope. Check that your friction device, rope grab and pulley all agree with the rope you actually climb on.

MRS climbers usually run a hitch cord or mechanical device, a micro pulley and a friction saver to protect the rope and the tree. SRS climbers add a rope wrench or SRT device, a chest harness and often a foot ascender. Spikes, which people also search as tree climbing spikes, live in the spurs department for removal work.

Good connectors are cheap insurance. Use auto-locking carabiners that need at least two deliberate actions to open in any life-support position, and keep a few non-locking carabiners and gear hooks on your saddle for tools. Swivels reduce twist in your lanyard or rope bridge, and rings make a clean, low-friction point for slings and bridges.
Brands like Notch, Petzl, DMM, ISC and CMI make most of the hardware in this section. Mixing brands is fine as long as each part is compatible and rated for the job.

Pulleys deserve a special mention. A micro pulley below your hitch makes slack tending smooth and saves your hitch cord, while a larger pulley can help with haul systems and rescue setups. Friction savers protect both rope and tree at your tie-in, and they make MRS climbing noticeably easier because the rope runs over metal or rings instead of bark.

Keep textiles out of the sun and away from bar oil, fuel and battery acid. Store rope in a bag, not loose in the truck bed. Inspect every device and connector before each climb, and log when life-support items went into service so you know when they are due for retirement under the manufacturer's guidelines.

Clean hardware with fresh water and let it dry fully. Lubricate gates and cams only with what the manufacturer recommends, and wipe away excess so it does not collect grit. Retire textiles that have been cut, glazed, chemically contaminated or shock loaded, and retire metal gear that is cracked, deformed or worn into sharp edges. The cost of replacing a piece of tree climbing gear is always smaller than the cost of trusting one that should have been retired.

faq.q: What is the most important piece of tree climbing gear?
faq.a: Every life-support component matters, but the parts that connect you to the rope, your friction device and connectors, deserve the most attention because they carry your full load on every climb.

faq.q: Can I mix gear from different brands?
faq.a: Yes, as long as each component is compatible with the others, rated for your rope diameter, and used according to its own manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: How often should I inspect climbing equipment?
faq.a: Before every climb, plus a more thorough documented inspection at regular intervals. Retire anything damaged, shock loaded or past the manufacturer's lifespan.

faq.q: Where are tree climbing spikes?
faq.a: Climbing spikes, also called spurs or gaffs, are in our spurs department along with replacement gaffs, pads and parts.

name: Ascent & Descent
title: Tree Climbing Ascenders and Descenders
meta: Tree climbing ascenders and descenders: hand ascenders, foot ascenders, rope grabs, belay and mechanical friction devices for MRS and SRS work.
intro: Tree climbing ascenders and descenders move you up the rope and bring you back down under control. This section covers hand and foot ascenders, rope grabs, figure 8s, belay devices and the mechanical friction devices that run MRS and SRS systems.

guide.h: Choosing gear for the way you climb
p: For SRS ascents, a hand ascender paired with a foot ascender or a chest-mounted device lets you walk up the rope efficiently. Descending and working the canopy is handled by your friction device, a rope wrench and hitch, or an all-in-one mechanical device. For MRS, ascent is usually done with a hitch and micro pulley, sometimes with a foot ascender added to save energy. Whatever you choose, confirm each device is rated for your rope diameter, use it per the manufacturer's instructions, get trained on it, and inspect it before every climb.

Coming down matters as much as going up. Mechanical friction devices and figure 8 descenders give smooth, controlled descents and can be set to add friction for heavier loads. Rope grabs help with positioning and lanyard adjustment, and a belay device can serve the ground crew during a rescue or when lowering a climber, where approved. Practice changeovers from ascent to descent low to the ground until they are second nature.

faq.q: Is a belay device the same as a climbing friction device?
faq.a: Not always. Some belay devices are approved for rope access or tree work, others are not. Check the manufacturer's instructions for the uses each device is approved for.

name: Foot Ascenders & Loops
title: Foot Ascenders & Foot Loops for Tree Climbing
meta: Foot ascenders and foot loops for SRS and MRS tree climbing. Compare right and left foot ascenders, knee ascenders and adjustable footloops.
intro: A foot ascender turns your legs into the engine of your climb, so you ride up the rope instead of pulling with your arms. We also carry foot loops for hand ascender setups and knee ascenders for rope walking systems.

guide.h: How foot ascenders and foot loops work
p: A foot ascender is a toothed cam device that straps to your boot. When you stand, it locks onto the rope; when you lift your foot, it slides up. Paired with a hand ascender or chest device on a stationary rope, it lets you climb in a smooth step-stand-step rhythm that saves your arms for the work at the top.

Foot loops are simpler. A footloop is a sling or adjustable strap that clips to a hand ascender so you can stand in it. Many climbers start with a foot loop and a hand ascender, then add a foot ascender once they are climbing SRS regularly.

guide.h: Right foot, left foot and knee ascenders
p: Most climbers run a foot ascender on the right foot, but left foot models exist, and some climbers run both for a rope walking style ascent. Knee ascenders mount higher on the leg and connect to the foot so the device moves with your knee, which some climbers find faster in long open ascents.
Match the device to your rope diameter and boot. A foot ascender should clamp snugly without crushing the boot, and the release should be easy to work with gloves on.

Rope matters as well. A foot ascender that grips cleanly on a firm, round 11.7 mm line may behave differently on a softer or fuzzier rope, so test it on the rope you actually climb before trusting it on a long ascent.

A foot ascender is not a life-support device on its own. It is there to help you climb, while your primary attachment stays on a device rated for life support. Keep the rope tended below you so the foot ascender feeds cleanly, and practice removing it while hanging before you need to do it high in a tree.
Inspect teeth, springs and straps before each climb. Worn or packed teeth slip, especially on muddy or icy rope.

If you are new to SRS, practice the whole ascent at low height with a trainer watching. It is easy to build a habit of loading the foot ascender awkwardly or letting slack build below your device, and both are much easier to correct on the ground than at the top of a tall tree. Wet, muddy or icy conditions call for extra attention, since teeth clog and grip falls off.

A common SRS ascent setup combines a hand ascender clipped to your bridge with a foot loop, a foot ascender on the right foot, and your friction device or rope wrench system already installed above. As you stand, the hand ascender slides up; as you sit, the friction device takes your weight. Some climbers add a chest harness with a chest ascender for a more efficient rope walk. Whatever you build, practice the full changeover from ascent to work mode close to the ground first.

Foot loops should be adjustable so you can set the height for your leg length. Too long and every step is wasted; too short and you cannot stand fully. Spend a few minutes tuning the length and the climb gets much easier.

faq.q: Do I need a foot ascender for SRS?
faq.a: No, but most SRS climbers use one because it makes long ascents faster and much less tiring than arm-heavy methods.

faq.q: What is the difference between a foot loop and a foot ascender?
faq.a: A foot loop is a strap you stand in, usually clipped to a hand ascender. A foot ascender is a cam device that grips the rope directly from your boot.

faq.q: Can I use a foot ascender for MRS?
faq.a: Some climbers add one to an MRS ascent to help advance the hitch, but always follow the device instructions and keep your life-support system primary.

faq.q: Do foot ascenders damage rope?
faq.a: Any toothed cam causes some wear. Use devices matched to your rope diameter, keep teeth clean, and inspect your rope regularly where the ascender runs.

name: Mechanical Friction Devices
h1: Mechanical Friction Devices & Climbing Friction Hitches
title: Mechanical Friction Devices vs Climbing Friction Hitches
meta: Mechanical friction devices that replace or work with climbing friction hitches. Compare MRS and SRS devices, rope wrenches and mechanical prusiks.
intro: Mechanical friction devices give you the control of climbing friction hitches with more consistent grab and release. Shop by system below: devices for MRS (moving rope) and devices for SRS (stationary rope).

p: Friction hitches for tree climbing, like the Distel or Valdotain tied in hitch cord, are light, cheap and adjustable, but they glaze, change with heat and moisture, and need a trained eye to dress and set. A mechanical prusik or friction device trades some cost and weight for repeatable behavior, smoother descents and easier one-handed tending. Many climbers run both: a device for daily work, and hitch cord kept in the kit. Whatever you use must be approved for life support by its manufacturer, matched to your rope, inspected before each climb, and learned under proper training.

Devices are usually built for one system. MRS devices work on a doubled rope that runs over your tie-in, while SRS devices work on a single fixed line, often with a rope wrench. Some can be configured for both with accessories. Start by choosing your system, then shop the matching subcategory below.
Read the device instructions closely for rope diameter and construction limits before you buy.

faq.q: Is a mechanical prusik safer than a friction hitch?
faq.a: Neither is automatically safer. Each is safe when correctly matched to the rope, set up per instructions and used by a trained climber.

faq.q: Can I use friction cord with a rope wrench?
faq.a: Yes. Many SRS setups use a rope wrench with a hitch tied in friction cord. Check that the cord, wrench and rope are compatible.

name: MRS Devices
title: Mechanical Prusik Devices for MRS Climbing
meta: Mechanical prusik devices for moving rope system tree climbing, including the Petzl Zigzag, Buckingham Throttle and Hitch Hiker 2, with fit and safety tips.
intro: A mechanical prusik for MRS replaces your hitch with a device that grips, releases and slack-tends predictably on a moving rope. These are built for doubled-rope climbing where the rope runs over your tie-in point.

p: Check the rope diameter range first, then how the device tends slack as you advance, how smooth it feels on descent, and whether you can operate it easily with gloves. Some devices pair with a pulley or chain of links for self-tending. Use each one only in the configurations its manufacturer approves, inspect it before every climb, and get trained on it before you rely on it in the tree.

Many MRS climbers start on a Valdotain or Distel hitch and move to a mechanical prusik as they climb more. The main draws are consistency, since a device does not change with heat, moisture or how well it was dressed, and smoother, more controllable descents. The trade-offs are weight, cost and the need to learn a new set of behaviors. Keep a hitch cord in your kit and stay fluent in tying hitches, because you never know when you will need a backup.

faq.q: Can MRS devices be used on SRS?
faq.a: Some can be converted with accessories, but not all. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for which systems each device is approved for.

name: SRS Devices
title: SRS Devices & Rope Wrenches for Tree Climbing
meta: SRS devices for stationary rope tree climbing: rope wrenches, adjustable rope wrenches and tethers that pair with a hitch for smooth descents and control.
intro: SRS devices let you work a stationary rope with control. The rope wrench family, including the ISC Rope Wrench and the Notch Flow, adds friction above a hitch so you can descend and move through the canopy smoothly.

p: A rope wrench rides above your hitch on a short tether and bends the rope through a few contact points, adding friction so the hitch does not have to do all the work. Adjustable wrenches let you tune friction for rope diameter, temperature and how heavy you are with tools. They work with a tether and a hitch, not instead of one.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions for compatible ropes, hitches and tethers, inspect wear points before every climb, and learn SRS from a qualified trainer.

Start by deciding how you want to climb. A rope wrench with a hitch is light and familiar to MRS climbers, and it suits climbers who want fine control. A tether choice matters too: rigid and semi-rigid tethers like the Notch Fusion keep the wrench aligned and help it tend itself. Consider how often you change between ropes of different diameters, and whether you want adjustable friction for different weather and rope conditions.

faq.q: Does a rope wrench replace my hitch?
faq.a: No. A rope wrench adds friction above a hitch or approved device. You still need the hitch or device as part of the life-support system.

name: Rope Grabs
title: Rope Grabs & Lanyard Adjusters for Arborists
meta: Rope grabs and lanyard adjusters for arborists: Petzl Micrograb, Climb Right rope grab and ART Positioner parts for positioning and lanyard control.
intro: A rope grab clamps onto a rope to hold your position or adjust a lanyard. In tree work the most common use is fine-tuning your flipline or lanyard length so you can lean back and cut with both hands.

p: Match the grab to the rope or lanyard diameter it will run on, and check whether it is approved for work positioning, fall arrest or both. Lanyard adjusters like the Petzl Micrograb are made for specific lanyard setups. Replacement cams and springs keep devices like the ART Positioner working. Inspect cams for wear and debris before every climb, and use each device only as its manufacturer intended.

Rope grabs rely on a cam and spring to bite the rope cleanly. Sawdust, sap and grit can pack into the cam teeth and reduce grip, so brush them clean regularly. Replacement cams, such as those for the ART Positioner, keep a good device in service longer. Retire any rope grab with a cracked body, worn cam or weak spring. When adjusting a lanyard under load, move smoothly and keep your hands clear of the cam.
Keep the device instructions in your kit so anyone inspecting it knows the approved uses and limits.

faq.q: Can a rope grab be used as my main climbing device?
faq.a: Only if the manufacturer approves it for that use. Most rope grabs sold for arborists are for lanyard adjustment and positioning.

name: Carabiners & Hardware
title: Carabiners & Climbing Hardware for Arborists
meta: Climbing carabiners and hardware for arborists: auto-locking, screw gate and non-locking carabiners, snap hooks, quick links and saddle storage clips.
intro: Carabiners are the small parts you clip a hundred times a day, so it pays to get the right ones. This section covers climbing carabiners for life support, gear carabiners for tools, snap hooks, quick links and saddle storage.

p: Not every carabiner belongs in your climbing system. For anything that holds you, ANSI Z133 calls for self-closing, self-locking connectors that take at least two deliberate actions to open, with a minimum breaking strength of 5,000 lbf (about 22.2 kN). In practice that means an auto-locking carabiner, usually a triple-action design, rated for climbing.

Non-locking and screw gate carabiners still have a place, just not as life support in a climbing line. They hang hand saws, water bottles, throw line bags and spare slings off your saddle. Keep the two jobs separate and mark or color-code them if it helps your crew.

Oval carabiners keep loads centered and work well with pulleys and rope wrenches. D and offset-D shapes put the load near the spine, where the carabiner is strongest, and give a wider gate opening. A pearabiner, or HMS shape, has a wide end that suits hitches and bulky connections such as a rope bridge.

Steel carabiners are heavier but handle wear from rope and hardware better, which makes them a good fit for rigging and high-wear points. Aluminum carabiners are lighter and are what most climbers carry on the saddle. Captive-eye or bar designs keep a carabiner oriented on a rope wrench or device.

Gate design matters too. Keylock noses avoid snagging on rope and slings. Wide gate openings make it easier to clip thick rope or a saddle bridge. Some carabiners have a captive bar or clip that holds a device or pulley in the correct orientation and prevents cross-loading.

Beyond carabiners, this section carries quick links and shackles for semi-permanent connections, connectors like the Notch Quickie for fast tie-ins, snap hooks for lanyards, and saddle storage hooks and clips. A good saddle storage setup keeps your carabiners, saws and slings in the same place every climb, which saves time and reduces dropped gear.
When you pick hardware, think about gate opening, gloved operation and whether a connector will stay oriented under load. Cross-loading, where the gate takes force, can drastically reduce strength.

Climbers often ask how many carabiners they need. A practical starting point is two or three auto-locking carabiners for your climbing system and lanyard, a spare locker for rescue or changes, and four to six non-locking or gear carabiners for tools and slings. Add more as your system grows.

Check every carabiner before use. The gate should close and lock on its own every time. Look for grooves worn by rope, sharp edges, cracks, corrosion or any distortion. Retire any connector that has been dropped onto a hard surface from height, shock loaded or that fails to lock fully. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for each model.
Keep a few spare lockers in your kit. A gate that sticks with sap or grit at the top of a tree is not something you want to discover without a backup.

faq.q: What carabiner do arborists use for climbing?
faq.a: For life support, arborists use self-closing, self-locking carabiners that need at least two deliberate actions to open and are rated for at least 5,000 lbf, which in practice means auto-locking climbing carabiners.

faq.q: Can I use a screw gate carabiner in my climbing system?
faq.a: Screw gate carabiners are not self-locking, so they do not meet Z133 for life-support connectors in a climbing line. Use them for gear and rigging where appropriate.

faq.q: What is a pearabiner?
faq.a: A pearabiner, also called an HMS carabiner, is a pear-shaped carabiner with a wide end that suits hitches, bridges and bulky connections.

faq.q: Are steel carabiners better than aluminum?
faq.a: Steel resists wear and abrasion better but weighs more. Aluminum is lighter and is the usual choice for carrying on a saddle.

name: Auto-Locking Carabiners
title: Autolock Carabiners for Tree Climbing
meta: Autolock carabiners for tree climbing from Petzl, DMM and Husqvarna. Triple-action auto locking climbing carabiners for life-support connections.
intro: An autolock carabiner closes and locks on its own every time you let go of the gate. For arborist life support, choose a triple-action auto locking carabiner rated for climbing, such as the Petzl Am'D or DMM Shadow.

p: In tree work you clip and unclip constantly, often while holding a saw or reaching around a limb. A screw gate can be left open by accident; an auto-locking carabiner cannot. ANSI Z133 calls for self-closing, self-locking connectors with at least two actions to open in life-support use. Pick a shape that suits the job, like an offset D for general use or an oval for pulleys, and check the gate operates cleanly with gloves. Inspect before every climb and retire any carabiner that does not lock fully.

Aluminum autolock carabiners like the DMM Shadow and Petzl Am'D are light enough to carry several on your saddle. Steel models handle wear better at high-friction spots. Look at gate opening for clipping thick rope, a keylock nose so it does not snag, and whether the shape works with your friction device or pulley. Locking carabiners for climbing should be checked for smooth gate action before every use, cleaned of sap and grit, and retired if the gate sticks or fails to lock on its own.

faq.q: What is the difference between twist-lock and triple-action carabiners?
faq.a: A twist-lock opens in two motions. A triple-action design adds a third step, usually lifting or pushing the sleeve, which helps prevent accidental opening from rope or bark rubbing the gate.

name: Quick Links & Hardware
title: Quick Links, Shackles & Climbing Hardware
meta: Climbing hardware for arborists: the Notch Quickie tie-in connector, Petzl Speedy link and stainless twisted shackles for bridges, slings and rigging.
intro: This climbing hardware covers the connectors that are not carabiners: quick-attach tie-in connectors, maillon-style links and shackles. They fill the gaps in a climbing or rigging setup where a carabiner is not the best fit.

p: A tie-in connector like the Notch Quickie lets you attach and detach your rope end quickly without a carabiner. Quick links and shackles make semi-permanent connections, such as fixing a pulley to a sling or closing a rope bridge setup, where you want a connector that will not open by accident. Check each piece's rating, use it only in the way its maker approves, keep threaded links fully closed, and inspect threads and pins before every use.

Stainless steel shackles and quick links resist corrosion and handle wear well, which makes them good for long-term setups like friction savers, rigging blocks or permanent anchors. Use pins and screw collars that close fully, and check them during the day, since vibration can loosen threads. Retire any piece with damaged threads, bent pins, cracks or wear grooves. Do not substitute generic hardware store links for rated climbing hardware in a life-support or rigging role.

faq.q: Can a quick link replace a carabiner?
faq.a: In some semi-permanent connections, yes, if it is rated for that use and fully closed. It is slower to open, so it is not ideal for connections you change often.

name: Non-Locking Carabiners
h1: Non Locking Carabiners for Gear & Tools
title: Non Locking Carabiners for Arborist Gear
meta: Non locking carabiners for racking tools, saws and slings on your saddle, including the Petzl Rollclip, DMM XSRE and Rock Exotica RockX accessory carabiners.
intro: Non locking carabiners keep your saddle organized. Use them to rack hand saws, slings, throw line and spare hardware, never as a life-support connector in your climbing system.

p: There are different types of carabiners for different jobs. A non locking carabiner is quick to clip with one hand, which is exactly why it is wrong for life support: a gate can be pushed open by a limb or rope. On the saddle, though, that speed is a plus. Pick rated climbing models over cheap keychain clips so they do not bend under a heavy saw, and give them a different color from your locking connectors so nobody grabs the wrong one.

A Petzl Rollclip has a built-in pulley, which can be handy for hitch tending in some setups when used as directed. Compact accessory carabiners, like the DMM XSRE or Rock Exotica RockX, are made for racking gear and save weight. Choose models with a gate that is easy to open with gloves and a keylock nose that will not snag on slings. Inspect them like any other carabiner, and retire any that are bent or have weak springs.

faq.q: Can I climb on a non locking carabiner?
faq.a: No. Life-support connectors in tree climbing must be self-locking. Non locking carabiners are for gear only.

name: Saddle Storage
title: Saddle Hooks, Chainsaw Hooks & Gear Clips
meta: Saddle hooks and gear clips for arborists: chainsaw hooks, rope holders, lanyard management clips and tool hangers that keep your saddle organized.
intro: A good saddle hook gives every tool a home. Chainsaw hooks, lanyard clips and rope holders keep your saw, flipline and spare rope where you can find them without looking.

p: Climbers who stay organized aloft tend to rack gear the same way every time. A dedicated chainsaw hook keeps a top-handle saw hanging clear of your rope, ready to grab. A lanyard management clip, such as the ISC Nessie, keeps the tail of your lanyard out of the way. A large tool hook like the Rock Exotica Transporter can carry spare rope or a rigging setup to the top of the tree.
Think about which side you cut on, where your hand saw sits and which side your lanyard adjuster lives, then place hooks so nothing crosses over your primary rope or bridge.

Saddle rope holders and large hooks also help when you carry a rigging line or a second climbing rope into the tree. Keep the load balanced on both sides of your saddle so it does not pull you off center on long climbs.

Do a dry run on the ground. Hang everything you plan to carry, then sit in the saddle and reach for each item with your eyes closed. If you fumble for something, move it. A few minutes of setup saves a lot of frustration aloft.

Check that hooks fit the gear loops or rails on your saddle and that they are rated for the weight you will hang. These are storage points only, not life-support attachment points. Inspect plastic hooks for cracks, especially after cold weather, and replace anything that has started to deform under a heavy saw.
Saddle hunters also use similar gear hangers, but tree workers carry heavier loads like chainsaws, so pick hardware sized for arborist use.

Weight limits are worth a second look if you carry a full-size saw aloft. A hook that handles a hand saw all day may flex or crack under a heavy chainsaw. Pick a chainsaw hook made for that load, and check the mounting point on the saddle is rated to carry it too.

Dropped gear is a hazard to the ground crew. Use hooks with gates or retention where you can, tether hand saws, and keep the drop zone clear and communicated. A tidy saddle is part of a safe job site.

Count your gear before you go up and after you come down. It is an easy habit that catches a missing hook or a hand saw left in a crotch before it becomes a problem for the next person under the tree.

Polymer hooks are light and gentle on rope and tools. Metal tool hooks carry heavier loads like a full-size chainsaw. Clips with gates or spring keepers hold gear more securely when you invert or move through the canopy. Some climbers mix several types: a heavy chainsaw hook on one side, polymer hooks for slings and lanyards, and a gated clip for the hand saw tether.
Consider the gear loops on your saddle. Some saddles use rails that accept clip-on hooks, while others use fixed loops that work better with carabiner-style storage.
Replace worn or cracked hooks as soon as you notice them, and keep a spare or two in your gear bag.

faq.q: What is a saddle hook used for?
faq.a: A saddle hook hangs tools and gear, such as a chainsaw, rope or lanyard, from the gear loops on your arborist saddle so your hands stay free.

faq.q: Can I clip my chainsaw to any carabiner?
faq.a: Use a hook or carabiner that fits your saw's lanyard and the saddle attachment. Many climbers prefer a dedicated chainsaw hook or a chainsaw lanyard so the saw hangs clear of their rope.

faq.q: Are saddle hooks life-support rated?
faq.a: No. Storage hooks and clips are for gear only. Never attach your climbing system to them.

name: Screw Gate Carabiners
title: Screw Gate Carabiners for Rigging and Gear
meta: Screw gate carabiners from Petzl and SMC for rigging, gear hauling and fixed connections. Learn where a screw gate fits and where an autolock is required.
intro: A screw gate carabiner locks with a threaded sleeve you turn by hand. It is a strong, simple connector for rigging, hauling gear and semi-permanent setups, but it is not a self-locking life-support connector under ANSI Z133.

guide.h: When to use a screw gate
p: Screw gates shine where a connection is made once and left alone, such as fixing a pulley to a sling in a rigging setup or closing a haul bag. They are inexpensive and often stronger than auto-lockers in the same size. Large steel screw gates, like the SMC heat-treated steel model, are popular for rigging because they shrug off wear. Always screw the sleeve fully closed, check it during the job, and keep auto-locking carabiners in your climbing system.

Aluminum screw gates are light and good for gear and slings. Steel screw gates are heavier but tough and wear resistant, which suits rigging blocks, slings and other places where rope runs through the carabiner. HMS shapes, like the Petzl William, handle bulky connections and hitches. Inspect threads and sleeves for grit, keep them clean and dry, and retire any carabiner with damaged threads or a gate that will not close smoothly.

faq.q: Why can't I use a screw gate carabiner for climbing?
faq.a: Z133 requires life-support connectors to be self-closing and self-locking. A screw gate depends on you to lock it, so it does not qualify.

name: Snap Hooks
title: Locking Snap Hooks & Climber Hooks for Arborists
meta: Locking snap hooks for arborist lanyards and climbing lines: double-locking aluminum and steel rope snaps plus the Petzl Eashook. Fit and inspection tips.
intro: A locking snap hook is the classic connector at the end of a lanyard or climbing line. Self-closing, double-locking rope snaps clip fast with one hand and stay put on your saddle D-rings.

p: Many climbers prefer a snap hook on the end of a flipline or lanyard because it is quick to clip and unclip with one hand, and its shape sits well on a saddle D-ring without rolling. Carabiners have larger gate openings and handle more types of connection. Both are common in tree work; what matters is that any snap hook in a life-support role is self-closing and self-locking with at least two deliberate actions to open, as ANSI Z133 calls for.
Old-style single-action snaps, sometimes still found on vintage climber hooks and gear, do not meet that requirement and should not be used for life support.
Snap hooks are also common on chainsaw lanyards, fall protection lanyards for aerial lifts and rigging lines, each with its own requirements. Make sure the snap you choose is rated for its role.

Climber hooks with a large gate opening also help when clipping around a thick stem or a wide saddle ring with gloves on. Try the gate with the gloves you actually wear before buying a set for the crew.

Steel rope snaps are heavier but very durable, and they hold up well on lanyards that see daily abuse. Aluminum double-locking snaps save weight on a long climbing day. Open-style hooks like the Petzl Eashook are designed to work with specific rope terminations, so check compatibility before you buy.
Look at gate opening size, whether the snap fits your saddle rings and lanyard eye, and how easy the lock is to release with gloves.

Snap hooks with a locking feature are sometimes sold as snap hook with lock or locking snap hook. Either way, check the rating and the number of actions needed to open it before using it for life support.
Weight differences add up when you carry several snaps on a lanyard and a climbing line.

Check that the keeper and gate close and lock on their own every time. Look for rope wear grooves, cracks, bent gates, worn pivots and corrosion. Retire any snap that sticks open, has been shock loaded or shows deformation. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for service life.

Clean snaps with fresh water if they get sticky with sap or grit, dry them fully, and use only the lubricant the manufacturer recommends. A snap that is slow to close is a snap that needs attention before the next climb.

guide.h: Fitting a snap to your line
p: Snaps are attached to a lanyard or rope with a sewn or spliced eye. A splice that is too loose lets the snap rotate and cross load; one that is too tight wears the rope. Many climbers buy lanyards with snaps already installed, or have them professionally spliced. If you replace the rope on an older lanyard, you can reuse the snap only if it passes inspection.

Think about how the snap will sit on your saddle. Some D-rings accept a snap better than a carabiner, while others work best with a narrow gate. Check that the snap cannot roll onto its gate or be cross loaded.

faq.q: What is a locking snap hook?
faq.a: It is a self-closing hook with a gate that locks automatically and needs at least two separate actions to open, so it cannot be opened by accidental contact.

faq.q: Can I put a snap hook on my climbing line?
faq.a: Yes, many climbers do, as long as the snap is life-support rated, self-locking and compatible with the rope termination and saddle hardware.

faq.q: What are climber hooks?
faq.a: People use the term for different things, including snap hooks for lanyards and the spurs used on poles and trees. For spurs, see our climbing spurs department.

name: Chainsaw Lanyards
title: Chainsaw Lanyards & Chainsaw Straps for Climbers
meta: Chainsaw lanyards and chainsaw straps for climbing arborists, including bungee lanyards with snaps, modular systems and the Weaver chainsaw strap.
intro: A chainsaw strap or lanyard tethers your saw to your saddle so you can cut, let go and keep both hands for climbing. Bungee models stretch with you and keep slack out of the way.

p: Length matters most. Too short and the saw fights you as you reach; too long and it swings into your rope or legs. Bungee lanyards keep the saw close when idle and stretch when you need reach. Use a snap or carabiner that fits your saw's attachment point and saddle hook. A saw lanyard is for the saw, not for you, so never clip your climbing system to it. Inspect stitching and bungee for cuts after every job, since it lives right next to the chain.

Bungee lanyards stretch when you reach and pull back when idle. Modular systems let you swap the lanyard between saws or attach points. A fixed strap, like the Weaver chainsaw strap, is simple and tough. All three ways to end a lanyard, whether a snap, a carabiner or a sewn eye, should fit your saw's attachment point. Avoid lanyards that let the saw hang below your feet or close to your climbing line.

faq.q: Do I need a chainsaw lanyard?
faq.a: If you run a saw in the tree, yes. A tethered saw protects the crew below and lets you use both hands to move.

name: Fliplines & Lanyards
title: Tree Climbing Lanyards & Arborist Fliplines
meta: Tree climbing lanyards and arborist fliplines: wire core, rope and 2 in 1 lanyards, pole straps and adjustable kits for positioning and removals.
intro: A tree climbing lanyard, often called a flipline, wraps the stem and holds you in position so you can cut with both hands. We carry rope, wire core and 2 in 1 designs plus adjustable kits.

p: Rope lanyards are light, flexible and easy to adjust. A wire core flipline has a steel cable inside for cut resistance when you work close to the saw on removals. A 2 in 1 lanyard puts a second attachment point on the same line so you can stay connected while passing limbs. Pick a length that suits your trees, add an adjuster for fine positioning, and remember a wire core is cut resistant, not cut proof. Inspect before every climb and follow Z133 by staying tied in twice when cutting.

Most arborist fliplines run 8 to 16 feet. Longer lines wrap big stems; shorter ones are easier to handle on small trees. Adjusters include mechanical rope grabs, friction hitches with a micro pulley and dedicated wire-core adjusters. An adjustable pole strap is a simpler option for utility work. Whatever you choose, make sure the adjuster is rated for your lanyard diameter, and keep a stopper at the end of the line.

faq.q: What is the difference between a flipline and a lanyard?
faq.a: The terms overlap. A flipline usually means a lanyard you flip around the trunk while climbing spars, while lanyard covers any adjustable positioning line.

name: Lanyard Kits
title: Climbing Lanyard Kits & Wire Core Assemblies
meta: Climbing lanyard kits with adjusters and connectors: wire core flipline kits and Petzl Grillon and Zillon positioning lanyards ready to clip on.
intro: A climbing lanyard kit gives you the line, adjuster and connectors in one ready-to-use setup. Choose a wire core flipline kit for removals or a Petzl Grillon or Zillon for everyday positioning.

p: A complete kit takes the guesswork out of matching the lanyard diameter to the adjuster and the connectors to your saddle. Wire rope lanyard assembly kits pair cable-core line with a matched adjuster and snaps. Mechanical positioning lanyards adjust smoothly with one hand under load. Confirm the length suits your trees, read the instructions for each component, and inspect the whole assembly before every climb.

Wire core kits suit removal climbers who spend time near the saw. Rope-based mechanical lanyards suit pruning and canopy work. Some kits are designed for specific saddles or snaps, so check the connector type. Make sure the kit's length suits the trees you climb and that the adjuster is easy to work with gloves. Store lanyard kits clean and dry, and replace any component that fails inspection with a matched part.

Kits also make good spares for the truck. When a lanyard gets nicked by a saw mid-job, a complete replacement lets the climber get back to work without improvising a setup from loose parts, which is never a good idea with life-support gear.

faq.q: What length climbing lanyard should I get?
faq.a: Most climbers use something in the 8 to 16 foot range. Longer lanyards suit big stems; shorter ones are easier to manage on smaller trees.

name: Rope Lanyards
title: Rope Lanyards for Tree Climbing & Arborists
meta: Rope lanyards for tree climbing arborists: replacement lanyard rope, Micrograb add-on kits and magnetic lanyard management. Buying tips from tree people.
intro: A rope lanyard is the everyday positioning tool for most tree climbers: light, adjustable and easy on the hands. We carry replacement lanyard rope, adjuster add-on kits and gear to keep your arborist lanyard tidy.

guide.h: Why most climbers run a rope lanyard
p: For pruning and general canopy work, a rope tree lanyard does nearly everything you need. It wraps a limb or stem, adjusts quickly, and is easy on bark and hands. Most climbing lanyards are made from the same kinds of arborist rope you climb on, often 11 to 13 mm, so they handle well with familiar hitches and mechanical adjusters.

For heavy removal work near the saw, many climbers switch to a wire core flipline for cut resistance. A rope lanyard is the better pick for most other work because it is lighter and gentler on the tree.
A rope lanyard also doubles as a second attachment point when you need to reposition your climbing line, which is why many climbers keep it clipped and ready at all times.

A tree lanyard also helps on big limb walks, where you can choke it around a lead above you for a second point of support while you reach out to make a cut. It gives a stable work position without relying on your climbing line alone, which is especially useful on long horizontal limbs.

There are two common ways to adjust a lanyard. A friction hitch tied with hitch cord, often with a micro pulley to tend slack, is light and cheap. A mechanical adjuster like the Petzl Micrograb gives fast one-handed adjustment and smooth release. An add-on kit lets you build a mechanical setup on your own lanyard rope.
Whichever you choose, match the adjuster to the lanyard diameter, keep a stopper knot or termination at the tail, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for the system.
Practice adjusting the lanyard while hanging in your climbing system before using it at height. The motion should be smooth and controllable with one hand.

A replacement rope lanyard without snaps lets you reuse your existing connectors and adjuster, provided they still pass inspection. Lanyard management clips and magnetic systems keep the tail coiled and out of your way so it does not snag on limbs or tangle with your climbing line.
Length is personal. Most climbers like a lanyard long enough to wrap the biggest stems they work on, typically 8 to 16 feet, with the tail managed so it does not hang in the way.
If you build your own, use a rope the adjuster maker approves and have terminations made by a qualified splicer or buy them pre-made. Life-support terminations are not the place to experiment.

Check the full length before every climb for cuts, glazing, flat spots, contamination and worn terminations. A lanyard lives near the saw, so it takes nicks; retire it at the first sign of a cut into the core. Per ANSI Z133, stay secured by two attachment points when operating a chainsaw in the tree.
Wash a dirty lanyard per the rope maker's instructions and let it dry away from direct heat or sunlight.

faq.q: What rope is best for a lanyard?
faq.a: Most climbers use an arborist climbing rope around 11 to 13 mm that matches their adjuster and hitch. Check the adjuster's approved diameter range.

faq.q: Rope lanyard or wire core flipline?
faq.a: Rope lanyards are lighter and better for pruning and general work. Wire core fliplines add cut resistance for removal work close to the saw.

faq.q: How do I adjust a rope lanyard?
faq.a: Use a friction hitch with a micro pulley or a mechanical adjuster such as a Micrograb. Both let you shorten and lengthen the lanyard while positioned.

name: Friction Savers
title: Friction Savers for Tree Climbing Arborists
meta: Friction savers for tree climbing: adjustable friction savers, ring-and-ring slings, anchor slings and the ART Ropeguide to protect rope, tree and climber.
intro: A friction saver sits between your rope and the tie-in limb, protecting the bark and your rope while making MRS climbing smoother. We carry adjustable friction savers, anchor slings and ring-style designs.

p: Running a rope directly over bark wears the rope, heats it, and damages the cambium. An arborist friction saver gives the rope a smooth metal or ring path, cuts friction so advancing your hitch is easier, and keeps the tie-in clean. Adjustable friction savers fit a range of limb diameters, and cambium savers with rings can often be retrieved from the ground. Size the sling to the limb, rate it for life support, and inspect before every climb.

Ring-and-ring friction savers use two rings on a sling; they are light, cheap and simple. Adjustable friction savers let you set the length to fit different limb sizes. Anchor slings with steel or aluminum rings can be girth-hitched or wrapped around a stem. Some designs, like the ART Ropeguide, add a pulley for smoother rope travel. Retrievable designs can be set and retrieved from the ground with the right technique. Inspect slings and rings for wear before every climb.

faq.q: Do I need a friction saver for SRS?
faq.a: Not always, because SRS anchors are often set differently, but many climbers still use an anchor sling or friction saver to protect the tree and rope.

name: Gear Storage
h1: Climbing Rope Storage, Rope Bags & Gear Bags
title: Climbing Rope Storage, Gear Bags & Organizers
meta: Climbing rope storage and gear organizers for arborists: rope bags, haul bags and duffels that keep rope clean, dry and ready for the next job.
intro: Good climbing rope storage keeps your life-support gear clean, dry and out of the truck bed. Choose rope bags for individual lines and larger gear bags for saddles, hardware and the rest of your climbing kit.

p: Rope and textiles fail from what happens between climbs as much as from climbing. Sunlight, bar oil, fuel, battery acid and grit all shorten their life. A rope left loose in a truck bed picks up sawdust and grit that work into the core and wear it from the inside. Proper climbing equipment storage is one of the cheapest ways to make gear last longer.
Bags also speed up the job. When each rope lives in its own bag and the saddle and hardware ride in a dedicated gear bag, setup at the tree is quick and you are less likely to leave something behind.
Storage is also part of an inspection routine. If every rope has its own bag and every bag has a tag with the rope's length and date in service, it is easy to see what is due for a closer look.

A rope bag is sized for one or two climbing lines and usually has a wide mouth and a ground tarp or base so you can feed rope straight out of it. A gear bag or haul bag is larger and tougher, built to carry saddles, helmets, connectors and devices. Some climbers use a tarp-style bag that opens flat to keep rope off the ground at the base of the tree.
Think about the size of your kit, whether you hike into jobs, and whether you want backpack straps or a simple duffel. Bright colors are easier to spot in the brush pile.

For crews, consistent storage across the truck pays off. Keep the same bag style for each climber's rope and the same bag for rigging lines, labeled clearly, so anyone on the crew can find the right line in a hurry.

A simple climbing gear organizer system helps: one bag per rope, labeled by length, and a separate bag for hardware. Keep a small pouch for spares like hitch cord and a backup carabiner. Store everything dry and out of direct sun, and never in the same compartment as fuel or bar oil.
Many climbers also use a rope tarp at the base of the tree. It keeps rope and gear off dirt, sap and rainwater, makes it easier to see what is laid out, and folds up quickly at the end of the job.

Packing up is a good time for a quick look at your gear. Flake rope into the bag and run it through your hands to feel for flat spots or damage. Note anything suspect and remove it from service until it can be inspected properly.
If you find contamination such as fuel or oil on a life-support textile, retire it. These chemicals can weaken fibers in ways you cannot see.

faq.q: How should I store climbing rope?
faq.a: Clean, dry, out of direct sunlight and away from fuel, oil and chemicals. A rope bag keeps it protected and ready to deploy.

faq.q: What is the difference between a rope bag and a gear bag?
faq.a: A rope bag is sized to hold and deploy a climbing line. A gear bag or haul bag is larger and carries saddles, helmets and hardware.

faq.q: Can I wash rope bags?
faq.a: Most can be rinsed or hand washed. Follow the maker's care instructions and let the bag dry fully before storing rope in it.

name: Gear Bags
h1: Climbing Gear Bags & Arborist Haul Bags
title: Climbing Gear Bags & Arborist Haul Bags
meta: Climbing gear bags and arborist haul bags from Buckingham, Edelrid and Petzl. Rugged bags to carry saddles, rope, hardware and helmets to the job.
intro: A climbing gear bag keeps your saddle, rope, hardware and helmet together, protected and easy to carry. We carry arborist haul bags and large duffels from Buckingham, Edelrid and Petzl.

guide.h: What makes a good arborist gear bag
p: Tree work is hard on bags. Look for heavy coated fabric that sheds water and sap, a stiff base so the bag stands open, and a wide opening so you can see what is inside. Backpack straps help when the job is a long walk from the truck. A drain grommet lets water out if the bag gets rained on.

Size the bag to your full kit. Most climbers carrying a saddle, one rope, a helmet and hardware need something in the medium to large range. A large duffel works well as a truck bag holding everything for a crew climber.

Inside pockets and loops help keep small items like hitch cord, spare carabiners and a first aid pouch from disappearing into the bottom of the bag. A light-colored lining makes it easier to see what is inside.

Arborist bags take more abuse than most climbing bags. They get dragged through brush, tossed in truck beds and left in the rain, so the toughest fabric you can afford usually pays for itself. Inspect seams and zippers each season and repair or replace before they fail.

A haul bag is a tall, tough cylinder with shoulder straps, built for dragging and hauling. It is a great arborist rope bag for a longer line plus some hardware. A duffel opens wide and suits a full kit you want to lay out on a tarp at the tree. Many climbers own one of each.
A small rope bag inside a big gear bag is a good combination: rope stays protected and ready to deploy, and everything else rides in the larger bag.

Keep sharp items like hand saws and spurs in their own scabbards or a separate bag so they do not cut rope or textiles. Keep fuel, bar oil and battery packs out of the gear bag entirely. Dry the bag and the gear inside after wet jobs before closing it up for storage.
Use packing time for a quick look at your gear. Anything damaged should be tagged and kept out of the bag until it is properly inspected or retired.
Label bags with the climber's name or crew number so gear does not wander between trucks. A tag on the handle is enough.

Buckingham haul bags are simple and tough, built for crews. The Edelrid Kurt haul bag is designed to stand up and open wide for rope and gear. The Petzl Duffel 85 is a large-capacity bag that also works as a travel bag for climbing competitions or long jobs. Pick based on how you carry your kit and how much space it needs.
Whatever you choose, look for reinforcements at the base and handles, since that is where bags fail first.
Hang gear bags open to air out at the end of a wet week.

faq.q: How big a climbing gear bag do I need?
faq.a: Lay out your full kit and pick a bag with room to spare. Most climbers want a medium to large haul bag or duffel for saddle, rope, helmet and hardware.

faq.q: Can I store rope in a gear bag?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the rope is kept separate from sharp tools, fuel and oil. Many climbers keep rope in its own rope bag inside or next to the gear bag.

faq.q: Are waterproof bags worth it?
faq.a: Coated, water-resistant bags help keep rope and textiles dry, but always dry gear thoroughly after wet jobs before storing it.

name: Rope Bags
title: Climbing Rope Bags for Arborists
meta: Climbing rope bags for arborists from Courant and Treehog. Rope bags that keep lines clean, deploy without tangles and protect your rope between jobs.
intro: A rope bag keeps your climbing line clean and lets it feed out tangle-free at the base of the tree. Pick a size that fits your rope length and diameter with a little room to spare.

p: Volume is usually listed in liters. Small rope bags suit short lanyards, throw line or a short climbing line, while larger ones hold a full-length climbing rope. Thicker rope and longer lengths need more room. Look for a stiff mouth that stays open, a stuff-not-coil design so you can feed rope in fast, and a tie-off loop for the tail. Keep each climbing rope bag free of fuel, oil and sharp tools, and inspect the rope as you flake it in.

A good rope bag has a strong base, sturdy handles or shoulder straps, and a closure that keeps rain and sawdust out. Many have a separate pocket for small hardware. Some, like the Courant Cargo and Cross bags, come in several sizes so a crew can match the bag to each rope. A tie-off point inside lets you keep the rope end accessible for setting a line. Bright colors stand out against brush and leaves, which helps when bags are spread around a site.

faq.q: Should I coil or stuff my rope into a bag?
faq.a: Stuffing the rope in loosely, end first, usually deploys with fewer tangles than coiling, and it is much faster.

name: Hitch Cord & Split Tails
h1: Hitch Cord & Split Tails for the Distel Hitch
title: Hitch Cord & Split Tails for the Distel Hitch
meta: Hitch cord and split tails for the Distel hitch, Valdotain and other climbing friction hitches. Yale Beeline split tails and spliced eye and eye cords.
intro: Hitch cord is the heart of a traditional climbing system. Tie a Distel hitch, VT or other friction hitch with a split tail or eye and eye cord matched to your climbing rope.

p: A hitch cord should be smaller in diameter than your climbing line and built to handle the heat of descents, which is why many are made with aramid or high-heat covers. An 8 mm cord on an 11 to 13 mm rope is a common starting point. A split tail is a length of cord with one terminated end that you tie into the hitch; an eye and eye has sewn or spliced eyes at both ends. Test any new hitch low and slow, retire glazed or stiff cord, and learn hitches under proper training.

guide.h: Split tail or eye and eye
p: A split tail is tied directly into your hitch and is easy to adjust. An eye and eye cord has terminated ends that clip into a carabiner, which makes setup cleaner and helps with hitch tending using a pulley. Popular cords include the Yale Beeline in 8 mm, made with a high-heat cover. Practice tying and dressing your preferred hitch until it is consistent, and replace cords when they become glazed, stiff or fuzzy.

faq.q: What is a Distel hitch?
faq.a: It is a common climbing friction hitch tied with a hitch cord onto the climbing rope. It grips under load and slides when tended or released.

name: Eye & Eye Prusiks
h1: Eye and Eye Prusiks & Hitch Climber Kits
title: Eye and Eye Prusiks & Hitch Climber Kits
meta: Eye and eye prusik cords, DMM Hitch Climber kits and hitch breakers for arborists. Spliced hitch cord that ties clean, consistent friction hitches.
intro: An eye and eye prusik is hitch cord with a terminated eye at each end, ready to tie a Valdotain, Distel or similar hitch. Pair it with a micro pulley and a hitch climber kit for a smooth MRS setup.

p: Length depends on the hitch you tie and the rope diameter you climb. Spliced eyes are slimmer and fit through pulleys and carabiners easily; sewn eyes are common too. A hitch breaker sits above the hitch so it releases more smoothly. A hitch climber kit bundles a pulley, connectors and cord into one matched setup. Inspect cords for glazing and stiffness, follow each part's instructions, and test new setups close to the ground.

A hitch climber pulley, like the DMM Hitch Climber, clips between the eyes of your eye and eye prusik and attaches to your bridge. This keeps the hitch in line and lets you tend slack smoothly with one hand. A hitch breaker, such as Big Jim's, sits on top of the hitch to make releasing it easier on descents. Hand-spliced eyes, like the Yale Beeline, are slim and consistent. Set up and test any new combination low to the ground.

faq.q: How long should an eye and eye prusik be?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and rope diameter. Many climbers use around 28 to 32 inches for a VT on 11 to 13 mm rope, then adjust to taste.

name: Micro Pulleys
title: Climbing Pulleys & Micro Pulleys for Arborists
meta: Climbing pulleys and micro pulleys for tree climbing: hitch-tending pulleys from DMM and CMI for MRS, lanyard and rescue setups. Selection tips.
intro: A micro pulley tends your hitch so you can pull slack one-handed while you climb. These compact climbing pulleys from DMM and CMI are built for hitch tending, lanyards and light hauling.

p: The most common arborist use is a pulley clipped below your friction hitch so you can tend slack as you advance. Check that the pulley side plates fit the hitch cord eyes and connectors, and that the sheave suits your rope diameter. Eccentric and hitch climber designs keep the hitch and pulley aligned. For rescue and light hauling, choose a pulley rated for those loads. Inspect sheaves and side plates before every climb.

Micro pulleys usually have aluminum side plates and a sheave on a bushing or bearing. Bearings run more smoothly but cost more. Eccentric pulleys, like the DMM Hitch Climber Eccentric, have a connection point that keeps the pulley oriented with your hitch. Rescue pulleys, like the CMI micro rescue pulley, are built for higher loads. Check ratings and compatibility with your hitch cord and connectors.
Keep sheaves free of sawdust and grit, and retire any pulley with cracked plates, a wobbling sheave or a worn axle. Micro pulley tree climbing setups only work well when the pulley spins freely.

faq.q: Do I need a pulley for my hitch?
faq.a: It is not required, but a micro pulley makes slack tending much easier and reduces wear on your hitch cord.

name: Other Climbing Gear
title: Tree Climbing Accessories & Specialty Gear
meta: Tree climbing accessories that do not fit anywhere else: the DMM Captain Hook, the Sawpod chainsaw holster and soft canopy anchors for arborists.
intro: This is the shelf for useful tree climbing accessories that do not fit a neat category: the Sawpod saw holster, the DMM Captain Hook and soft canopy anchors.

p: A dedicated saw holster keeps a top-handle saw secure on your saddle when it is not running. A large gear hook carries rope or a rigging setup up the tree. A soft canopy anchor is a textile anchor you can set around a stem or limb for a tie-in. Each of these makes a common task safer or faster. Check whether an item is rated for life support or for gear only, follow its instructions, and inspect it with the rest of your kit.

The best accessories solve a problem you run into often. If you climb with a top-handle saw, a holster like the Sawpod keeps it secure. If you carry heavy gear aloft, a big hook like the DMM Captain Hook spreads the load. If you set many anchors, a soft canopy anchor gives you a quick, rated option. Avoid adding gear just because it is new; more items on your saddle means more weight and more things to snag.

faq.q: Is a soft canopy anchor life-support rated?
faq.a: Rated textile anchors are designed for life support when used as directed. Always confirm the rating and instructions for the specific product.

name: Rings
title: Climbing Rings for Bridges, Slings & Anchors
meta: Climbing rings for arborists from DMM and Petzl: anchor rings and open rings for rope bridges, friction savers and slings. Rated for life support.
intro: Climbing rings give a smooth, low-friction connection point for rope bridges, friction savers and anchor slings. We carry solid DMM anchor rings plus Petzl closed and open rings.

p: A ring on your saddle bridge lets your climbing system slide side to side as you move, and a pair of rings on a sling makes a simple retrievable friction saver. Open rings can be installed on a bridge or sling without unthreading it. Check the strength rating, match the inside diameter to the rope or sling, and inspect for grooves and sharp edges before each climb.

Solid aluminum rings, like the DMM anchor rings, are light and smooth. Steel rings resist wear better in high-friction spots. Petzl offers both closed rings and open rings that can be added to a bridge without removing it. Ring size matters: a larger inside diameter lets a rope run more freely. Retire any ring with deep wear grooves, cracks or sharp edges.

Rings used as a friction saver pair should be sized so the smaller ring passes through the larger one for retrieval. Check that combination before you head up the tree, and keep the instructions for each ring with your kit.

faq.q: What are climbing rings used for in tree work?
faq.a: Mostly for rope bridges on saddles and for ring-and-ring friction savers, where they give a smooth, strong connection.

name: Swivels
title: Climbing Swivels: Petzl, CAMP & CMI
meta: Climbing swivels for arborists, including the Petzl swivel range, the CAMP Enigma and the CMI California swivel. Reduce twist in your rope and lanyard.
intro: A climbing swivel lets your system rotate without twisting your rope, lanyard or bridge. We carry the Petzl Micro Swivel, the CAMP Enigma and the CMI California swivel.

p: Climbers often put a swivel between the bridge and their friction device so they can spin to face the work without twisting the rope. Swivels also help in rigging and rescue setups where loads rotate. Open-style swivels, like the Petzl Micro Swivel Open, can be attached to a bridge without removing it. Check the rating and compatibility with your connectors, and inspect the bearing for smooth rotation before every climb.

Small swivels like the Petzl Micro Swivel are light and compact for climbing systems. Larger swivels such as the CAMP Enigma and the CMI California swivel handle heavier loads and suit rigging and rescue. Look at the strength rating, the size of the attachment eyes and how freely it rotates. Some climbers prefer to avoid swivels in their climbing system to reduce weight and complexity; it is a personal choice.
Inspect swivels before every climb: they should turn smoothly without grinding, and the eyes should be free of wear grooves or cracks.

faq.q: Do I need a swivel on my saddle?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but many climbers like one to reduce rope twist and make turning in the tree easier.

name: Helmets
title: Arborist Helmets & Tree Trimming Helmet Systems
meta: Arborist helmets and tree trimming helmet systems from Petzl, Kask, Pfanner and Husqvarna. Climbing and forestry helmets with visors and hearing protection.
intro: A tree trimming helmet has to handle overhead strikes, side impacts and a full day on your head. We carry climbing-style arborist helmets plus forestry systems with built-in visors and hearing protection.

p: Climbing-style helmets like the Petzl Vertex Vent and Kask Super Plasma use a chinstrap to stay on during a fall and are common for climbers. Forestry systems often include a mesh visor and earmuffs, which suits ground crew and saw work. Look for the standards printed on the shell, such as ANSI Z89.1, and decide whether you need a vented or electrically rated helmet based on your work near power. Wear a properly fitted helmet whenever you are aloft or in the work zone, and replace it after a hard impact or as the manufacturer advises.

Many helmets accept clip-on visors and earmuffs, so you can build a full head protection system. A mesh visor keeps out sawdust and chips; a clear visor protects from fine debris. Earmuffs are essential around saws and chippers. Headlamps clip onto many climbing helmets for early starts and storm work. Make sure any accessory is compatible with your helmet model so it does not affect fit or protection.

faq.q: Can I use a regular hard hat for tree climbing?
faq.a: Many basic hard hats have no chinstrap and can come off in a fall. Climbing-style helmets are designed to stay on and are preferred aloft.

name: Saddles & Harnesses
title: Tree Climbing Harness & Arborist Saddle Guide
meta: Tree climbing harness and arborist saddle guide: Buckingham, Weaver, Petzl, DMM and Treemotion saddles plus chest harnesses, parts and accessories.
intro: A tree climbing harness is the piece of gear you spend the whole day sitting in, so fit and comfort matter as much as features. Compare arborist saddles from Buckingham, Weaver, Petzl, DMM and Treemotion, plus chest harnesses and parts.

p: In tree work, saddle and harness mean nearly the same thing: an arborist harness built for work positioning, with a wide waist belt, leg straps and attachment points for a climbing line and lanyard. What sets an arborist climbing harness apart from a rock climbing harness is support for hours of hanging, side D-rings for a lanyard, gear loops and rails for tools, and usually a rope bridge that lets your attachment point slide across the front.

Full body harnesses that include shoulder straps and a dorsal attachment are a different category, mainly for fall arrest in bucket trucks and aerial lifts. They are not a substitute for a work positioning saddle in the tree, and a tree saddle is not a fall arrest harness.

guide.h: How to choose a climbing saddle
p: Start with how you climb. A climber doing mostly removals on spurs wants a stiff, supportive saddle with wide leg pads and sturdy side D-rings. A pruning climber working SRS all day wants something lighter with good freedom of movement and a comfortable sit. Look at the bridge setup, whether you can adjust it, and how the leg straps attach.

Fit is everything. Measure your waist and thighs, check the sizing chart, and if possible try the harness on and hang in it. Pressure points that seem minor on the ground become miserable after six hours in a tree. Many saddles adjust widely, but the waist pad should sit comfortably above your hips.
Consider gear capacity too. Climbers who carry a lot of tools want plenty of loops and rails. Climbers who work light want a saddle that carries just the essentials without bulk.

Buckingham and Weaver build classic American saddles with a long track record in removals and utility work. European designs such as the Petzl Sequoia, DMM Kinisi and Treemotion focus on adjustability, light weight and a comfortable hang for long canopy days. Neither style is better in every case. Many experienced climbers own one of each for different kinds of work.

Chest harnesses, saddle parts and accessories round out the section. A chest harness helps keep you upright and is common in SRS setups, where it often carries an ascender. Replacement bridges, D-rings and leg straps keep a good saddle in service longer.
Weaver saddles are popular with utility and line clearance climbers. Full body harnesses are available in this section for aerial lift and rescue use, separate from tree climbing saddles.

Inspect your saddle before every climb: stitching, webbing, buckles, D-rings, bridges and gear loops. Look for cuts, abrasion, heat damage, chemical stains and worn or deformed hardware. Replace bridges on the schedule the manufacturer gives, or sooner if worn. Follow the manufacturer's lifespan guidance, keep the saddle away from fuel and oil, and make sure every climber is trained in its use and in the requirements of ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What is the best tree climbing harness for beginners?
faq.a: One that fits you well and suits the work you will do most. A mid-weight saddle with an adjustable bridge and good leg support is a comfortable all-round starting point.

faq.q: Can I use a rock climbing harness to climb trees?
faq.a: Rock harnesses are not designed for hours of work positioning and usually lack side D-rings for a lanyard. Use an arborist saddle for tree work.

faq.q: How often should I replace my saddle bridge?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's guidance and replace it sooner if you see abrasion, cuts, glazing or any damage. Bridges wear faster than the rest of the saddle.

faq.q: Is a full body harness better for climbing trees?
faq.a: Full body harnesses are mainly for fall arrest, such as in aerial lifts. For climbing, an arborist saddle, sometimes with a chest harness, is the standard choice.

name: Buckingham Saddles
title: Buckingham Saddles: Tree Climbing Saddles Compared
meta: Buckingham saddles compared: Agility, Buckcraft and Ergovation tree climbing saddles. Fit, features and which Buckingham saddle suits your work.
intro: Buckingham saddles have been on American tree crews for a long time, known for tough construction and solid support. Compare the Agility, Buckcraft and Ergovation to find the Buckingham tree saddle that suits how you climb.

p: The Buckcraft is a classic utility and removal saddle with a stiff back and a straightforward layout. The Agility is lighter and more flexible, aimed at climbers who spend their day moving through the canopy. The Ergovation focuses on comfort over long days, with a design built around keeping pressure off the hips and legs.
All three are work positioning saddles with side D-rings for a lanyard. Look at the attachment points, bridge options and gear storage to decide which matches your system.

If you are not sure which suits you, think about how you spend most of your time. Spur work and removals point toward the Buckcraft. Long canopy days on rope point toward the Agility or Ergovation. If you split time between both, comfort over long hangs is usually the deciding factor.

Buckingham tree climbing equipment has a long history in American tree care, and the saddles reflect that: thick padding, tough webbing and hardware sized for daily use. The trade-off is that some models are heavier than European alternatives. For many climbers, especially those doing removals, that durability is the point.

Buckingham climbing saddles come in sizes based on waist measurement. Measure over the clothes you actually work in, check the size chart, and leave room for adjustment. Leg straps should support your thighs without pinching, and the back should sit above your hips. If you can, hang in a saddle before committing to it for daily work.
Leg straps on Buckingham saddles adjust differently from model to model, so read the fit instructions. Some climbers add padding or adjust strap placement to suit their build.
