A good fit also improves safety, since a saddle that rides up or shifts can put you in awkward positions.

Buckingham also builds spurs, lanyards and bags, so some climbers keep their whole kit in one brand. That is not required. Any compatible, rated connector, lanyard or friction device can work with a Buckingham saddle as long as you follow each manufacturer's instructions.
Buckingham also makes replacement parts like bridges and D-rings for some models. Using genuine parts keeps the saddle within the manufacturer's approved configuration.
Mixing brands is common and works well when every part is compatible.

Inspect stitching, webbing, buckles and D-rings before each climb. Keep the saddle away from fuel, bar oil and battery acid, dry it out after wet days and replace worn bridges promptly. Retire the saddle according to Buckingham's guidance or if anything looks wrong. Train with the saddle before using it for real work, and follow ANSI Z133.

Keep the saddle's manual with your gear records. It contains the approved attachment points and inspection criteria for that model, which is exactly what you need when checking it before work or training a new climber on it.

faq.q: Which Buckingham saddle is best for removals?
faq.a: The Buckcraft has long been a favorite for removal and spur work thanks to its stiff, supportive design.

faq.q: Are Buckingham saddles good for SRS climbing?
faq.a: Yes, with the right bridge and attachment setup. Lighter models like the Agility suit climbers who move a lot in the canopy.

faq.q: How do I size a Buckingham tree saddle?
faq.a: Measure your waist over your work clothes and use Buckingham's size chart. Pick a size that leaves room to adjust.

name: European Saddles
title: European Climbing Saddles: Petzl, DMM, Treemotion
meta: European climbing saddles for arborists: the Petzl Sequoia, DMM Kinisi Max and Treemotion Pro. Lightweight, adjustable harnesses for long canopy days.
intro: A European climbing saddle trades bulk for adjustability and freedom of movement. The Petzl Sequoia, DMM Kinisi Max and Treemotion Pro are built for long days in the canopy, especially on SRS.

p: European-style saddles typically use lighter materials, a wide range of adjustment at the waist and legs, and bridge setups that let you swap or tune attachment points. Many climbers find they make SRS and canopy movement easier. Try the fit with your work clothes on, check that gear storage suits your tools, replace bridges per the maker's schedule, and inspect before every climb.

The Petzl Sequoia has a long history with arborists, with adjustable leg loops and a comfortable sit. The DMM Kinisi Max is built with SRS climbers in mind, with a focus on comfort and adjustability. The Treemotion Pro is known for its supportive design and wide range of customization. Each has its fans, so try one on if you can. Pay attention to bridge length, how attachment points sit, and how the gear loops work with your tools.

Many European saddles use replaceable bridges and modular parts, which helps them stay in service longer. Buy genuine replacement parts and follow the manufacturer's schedule for swapping bridges and other wear items.

faq.q: Are European saddles good for spur work?
faq.a: They can be, but some climbers prefer a stiffer American saddle for long days on spurs. Fit and personal preference decide it.

name: Saddle Parts & Chest Harnesses
title: Arborist Saddle Parts & Chest Harnesses
meta: Arborist saddle parts and chest harnesses: the Edelrid TreeRex bungee chest harness, Weaver chest box and SRT chest harnesses for your climbing setup.
intro: Arborist saddle parts and chest harnesses keep a good saddle working and make SRS climbing easier. A chest harness keeps you upright and often carries a chest ascender.

p: Chest harnesses come in bungee styles that stretch with you and fixed styles that hold an ascender in place. Confirm a chest harness or part is compatible with your saddle model. Replacement parts like bridges and leg straps should come from the saddle's manufacturer or be approved by them. Install per the instructions, inspect before every climb, and never improvise life-support parts.

The Edelrid TreeRex bungee chest harness stretches to keep you upright without restricting movement. The Weaver chest box is a sturdy option for utility climbers. SRT chest harnesses are designed to hold a chest ascender in line for efficient ascents. Check fit across your shoulders and how it connects to your saddle. A chest harness that is too tight restricts breathing; too loose and it does not keep the ascender aligned.

Knowing the parts of a saddle makes inspection easier: waist belt, leg straps, side D-rings, bridge, attachment rings and gear loops. Check each one before every climb and replace worn parts with approved ones.

faq.q: Does a chest harness make my saddle a full body harness?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Many arborist chest harnesses are for positioning and ascent only. Check the manufacturer's rating before relying on it for anything else.

name: Spurs
title: Arborist Spikes & Tree Climbing Spurs
meta: Arborist spikes and tree climbing spurs: aluminum and steel climbers, replacement gaffs, pads and straps from Buckingham, Climb Right, Notch and Distel.
intro: Arborist spikes, also called spurs or climbers, get you up a stem fast on removals and spar work. Compare aluminum and steel spurs, then keep them working with replacement gaffs, pads and straps.

p: Arborist spikes are for removals and for climbing trees that are coming down. Each gaff punches a wound through the bark, so climbing a tree with spurs that you intend to keep is poor practice, and ANSI A300 limits spur use for pruning to specific situations such as aerial rescue. On a removal, spurs combined with a flipline let you work down a spar quickly, while most climbers stay tied in with their climbing line as well, giving two points of attachment while cutting.

Aluminum spurs are lighter and easier on your knees over a long day; steel spurs are tougher and usually cost less. Fit the shank so it ends a few fingers below the knee, and pick wide pads that spread the load on your calf. Short gaffs suit thin-barked hardwoods, while longer gaffs reach through thick bark on conifers. Keep gaffs sharp with the maker's profile, wear stiff-shanked boots, learn spur climbing from a qualified trainer, and inspect straps, pads and gaffs before every climb.

faq.q: Can I use spurs to prune a tree?
faq.a: No. Spurs wound the tree and should only be used on removals, with limited exceptions such as an aerial rescue.

faq.q: What gaff length do I need?
faq.a: Short gaffs for thin-barked hardwoods, longer gaffs for thick-barked conifers. Many climbers keep both.

name: Aluminum Spurs
title: Aluminum Spurs: Lightweight Tree Climbing Spikes
meta: Aluminum spurs for tree climbing from Climb Right and Notch. Lightweight climbers with Big Buck or steel support pads for long removal days.
intro: Aluminum spurs cut weight off your legs, which adds up over a long day of removals. We carry Climb Right aluminum climbers with different pad options and the Notch Ergo climbers.

p: Every step on spurs means lifting the spur with your leg. Lighter aluminum shanks reduce fatigue in your hips and knees, so you climb fresher at the end of the day. For climbers who are on spurs most days, the savings are worth the extra cost over steel.
Aluminum shanks are strong but can be more prone to wear in some spots, so inspect them closely, especially around the gaff mount and strap slots.
Lighter spurs also help on spar work where you climb, cut, flip your lanyard and climb again many times in a day. Every ounce saved on each leg adds up across hundreds of steps.
For occasional spur users, steel may be the more economical choice. For daily removal climbers, aluminum spurs are often the first upgrade they make.

Pads spread pressure across your calves. Big Buck style pads are wide and supportive, while steel-support pads add stiffness for heavy climbers or long climbs. Make sure the shank length fits your leg; the top should sit a few fingers below the knee joint.
Adjust straps snug but not tight enough to restrict circulation. Replacement pads and straps are available when the originals wear out.

Look at the stirrup too. It should sit squarely under the boot's arch and shank, and the lower strap should hold it firmly without pressing on the top of your foot. A badly placed stirrup can make even the lightest spur feel unstable on the stem. Wear your usual climbing boots when fitting new spurs.

Choose a gaff length suited to the bark you climb, and keep it sharp with the correct profile. Replace gaffs when they wear short or get damaged. Inspect the whole spur before each climb, and only climb on spurs for removals, with proper training and a flipline.
Store aluminum spurs with gaff guards on so the points stay sharp and do not cut rope, bags or the climber reaching into the truck.
Carry a small file in the truck for touch-ups, following the maker's guidance for the correct gaff profile.

Climb Right aluminum climbers come with Big Buck pads or steel support pads, so you can pick the level of stiffness you want. Notch Ergo climbers are designed with an ergonomic shape for comfort on long days. Look at the shank shape, how the stirrup sits under your boot and the pad and strap system. Fit is personal, so try them on if you can and walk around before climbing.
Check that the climbers you choose accept the gaff length you want, and that replacement parts are available.
Before your first long day, wear the spurs for a few short climbs to set strap tension and pad position. Small fit problems become big ones over a full removal.

faq.q: Are aluminum spurs as strong as steel?
faq.a: Quality aluminum spurs are designed for full-time professional use. Steel resists wear better, while aluminum saves weight.

faq.q: Can I put different gaffs on aluminum spurs?
faq.a: Many models accept replacement gaffs in different lengths. Check compatibility with the spur's maker.

faq.q: Do aluminum spurs need different maintenance?
faq.a: Inspect shanks and gaff mounts closely for wear, keep gaffs sharp, and follow the manufacturer's care guidance.

name: Buckingham Steel Spurs
title: Buckingham Climbing Spikes: Steel Spurs
meta: Buckingham climbing spikes in steel: tree climbing spurs with Big Buck pads, T-pads or lower straps. Rugged, affordable spurs for removal work.
intro: Buckingham climbing spikes in steel are tough, proven spurs for removal work. Choose from setups with Big Buck pads, T-pads or lower strap configurations to suit your legs and climbing style.

p: Steel shanks add weight compared with aluminum but resist wear and often cost less, which suits crews that buy spurs for several climbers. Pick a pad style that spreads load comfortably on your calf, fit the shank length to your leg, and keep gaffs sharp with the correct profile. Use spurs only for removals, with a flipline and proper training, and inspect before every climb.

Buckingham steel climbers come with different pad setups. Big Buck pads are wide and supportive for long days. T-pads are a simpler, lighter option. Lower strap configurations change how the spur holds to your boot and ankle. Choose the setup that feels secure without pinching, and replace pads and straps when they wear. Keep gaffs sharp and retire any spur with a cracked shank or damaged stirrup.
Steel spurs are also a good backup set for the truck, so a broken strap or worn gaff on your main climbers does not stop a removal halfway through.

faq.q: Can I replace the gaffs on Buckingham steel spurs?
faq.a: Many Buckingham spurs accept replacement gaffs. Check the model and use compatible parts.

name: Climber Pads
title: Climber Pads for Tree Climbing Spurs
meta: Climber pads for tree climbing spurs, including Buckingham Big Buck pads and replacement pads for Gecko climbers. Better comfort on long spur days.
intro: Good climber pads spread the load of your spurs across your calf and make long removal days far more bearable. We carry Big Buck pads and replacement pads for Gecko climbers.

p: Pads come in different widths and stiffness. Wider pads spread pressure better, while stiffer pads with metal supports keep the spur from rolling on your leg. Make sure the pad fits your spur model, attaches securely, and works with your strap setup. Replace pads when the foam is crushed or the straps wear, and inspect everything before each climb.

Buckingham Big Buck pads are a popular upgrade for many spurs, with versions that use buckles or hook-and-loop closures. Replacement pads for Gecko climbers keep those spurs comfortable. When fitting new pads, adjust the straps so the spur sits snug against your leg without cutting off circulation. Worn pads let the spur shift and rub, which is both uncomfortable and less stable on the stem.
Keep pads clean and dry after use. Sap and mud stiffen padding and wear out straps, and wet pads can rub skin raw on long days. Replace both pads at the same time so your legs stay balanced.

faq.q: Do climber pads fit all spurs?
faq.a: No. Pads are often made for specific spur models. Check compatibility before buying.

name: Gaffs & Spur Parts
title: Climbing Gaffs & Replacement Spur Parts
meta: Climbing gaffs and replacement spur parts: Buckalloy tree gaffs, Edelrid Talon strap systems and Distel replacement pads with rings and straps.
intro: Replacement climbing gaffs and parts keep your spurs working longer. Swap worn or short gaffs, replace straps and pads, and change gaff length to suit the bark you climb.

p: Tree gaffs must match the mounting style of your spurs, such as screw-and-dowel or other systems. Short gaffs suit thin-barked hardwoods; longer gaffs reach through thick bark on conifers. Install gaffs per the maker's instructions, keep them sharp with the correct profile, and retire gaffs that are worn short, bent or cracked. Inspect straps and pads before each climb too.

Spur parts such as the Edelrid Talon upper strap system and Distel replacement pads with rings and straps let you rebuild worn spurs instead of replacing the whole set. Use parts made for your spur model. Bashlin gaffs and other brands may not be interchangeable, so check the mounting before you buy. Sharpen gaffs with a file using the correct profile, never on a grinder, which can overheat the steel.
If you are unsure about any part, ask the spur maker or take the spurs out of service until they can be checked. Spurs are life-critical gear when you are working a spar.

faq.q: When should I replace my gaffs?
faq.a: When they are worn below the manufacturer's minimum length, bent, cracked or cannot be sharpened to the correct profile.

name: Throw Weights & Line
title: Arborist Throw Weight & Throw Line
meta: Arborist throw weight and throw line for setting your climbing line, plus throw line storage cubes and launchers. Pick the right weight and line.
intro: A throw weight and throw line let you set your climbing line in the canopy from the ground. We carry arborist throw weights, throw line, storage cubes and launcher kits.

p: Throw weights usually range from about 8 to 16 ounces. Lighter weights travel farther and slip through small crotches but may not pull line down through rough bark; heavier ones fall more reliably. Many climbers carry two sizes. Pair the weight with a slick throw line that runs smoothly and stores tangle-free in a cube or bag. Make sure the drop zone is clear before every throw and never throw near power lines.

A throw line storage cube folds open on the ground so line feeds out without tangling, then folds closed for transport. Weights like the Petzl Jet have a rounded shape that slides through crotches and bark. Practice underhand and two-handed throws to place your line accurately. When the weight is over the right crotch, use it to pull up your climbing line or a heavier line, and check the crotch from different angles before you climb.
Always keep the ground crew clear while throwing.

faq.q: How heavy should my throw ball for tree work be?
faq.a: Most climbers start with something around 12 ounces and add a lighter and a heavier weight as needed.

name: Throw Line Kits
title: Throw Line Kits & Throw Line Launchers
meta: Throw line kits for arborists: starter kits with throw weights, line and a storage cube, plus the Big Shot throw line launcher for high tie-ins.
intro: A throw line kit bundles weights, line and a storage cube so you can start setting lines right away. For high tie-ins, a throw line launcher like the Big Shot reaches farther than throwing by hand.

p: A starter kit is the easiest way to begin: matched weights and arborist throw line with a cube that folds open for tangle-free deployment. A launcher uses a pole and band to send the weight much higher than a hand throw, which helps on tall trees. Launchers need care: clear the area, wear eye protection, keep everyone out of the line of fire, and follow the manufacturer's instructions.

A starter throw line kit typically includes one or two throw weights, a length of arborist throw line and a storage cube or bag. Some include a second line for setting two lines at once. Pick a kit with weights you will actually use and a line that suits your trees. Launchers like the Big Shot use a pole-mounted band to propel the weight. Inspect launcher bands and line for wear, and replace worn parts before they fail.
Keep the kit together in its bag so the cube, weights and line are ready on every job.

faq.q: Do I need a launcher?
faq.a: For most trees a hand throw is enough. A launcher helps on very tall trees or when you need to hit a precise high crotch.

name: Throw Line
title: Arborist Throw Line: Samson, Teufelberger & More
meta: Arborist throw line from Samson, Teufelberger and others: slick, low-stretch throwline that runs clean through crotches for setting climbing lines.
intro: Arborist throw line is a thin, slick cord that carries your throw weight into the canopy and pulls your climbing line up after it. We carry Samson Zing-It, Teufelberger Dynaglide and other throwline.

p: Good throw line is slick enough to run through crotches and over bark without hanging up, and stiff enough to resist tangling. Diameter is usually just under 2 to around 2.2 mm. Thinner line throws farther; thicker line is easier to handle. Bright colors help you see it in the canopy. Store it in a cube or bag, and replace it when the cover fuzzes or it starts to kink. Throw line is not life-support rope.

Samson Zing-It is a well-known slick throwline that resists abrasion. Teufelberger Dynaglide is another popular choice with very low stretch. Target line is a bright option designed for visibility in the canopy. Line length usually comes on spools long enough for tall trees. Pick a line that matches your throw weight and the height of the trees you climb. Keep a spare line in the truck so a damaged or stuck line does not stop the job.

faq.q: Can I use paracord as throw line?
faq.a: Paracord is rougher and stretchier, and it tends to hang up and tangle. Purpose-made arborist throw line runs much more cleanly.

name: Climbing Kits
title: Tree Climbing Gear Kits for Arborists
meta: Tree climbing gear kits for arborists: rope climbing kits that bundle the core gear for a working system, with advice on fit, training and upgrades.
intro: Tree climbing gear kits bundle the core arborist gear for a working climbing system, saving you the job of matching every rope, connector and device yourself. Start with a kit, then personalize it as you learn what you like.

p: A typical arborist rope climbing kit includes a climbing rope, a hitch cord or friction device, a micro pulley, connectors, and often a friction saver and throw line. Some kits add a saddle, lanyard and helmet. Check exactly what is in a kit before buying so you know what you still need to add.

The value of a kit is compatibility. The rope diameter, hitch cord, pulley and connectors are chosen to work together, which matters a lot when you are new and do not yet know which combinations behave well.
Rope length is another thing to check. Climbing rope comes in lengths that suit different tree heights, and a kit rope should be long enough for the trees you work in with some extra for tying off.
Check whether connectors in the kit are auto-locking and rated for climbing, and that the rope and hitch cord come with terminations finished by a qualified maker.

Experienced climbers often build their own setup piece by piece. For a newer climber or a crew outfitting a new hire, a kit gets reliable arborist tree climbing gear into service quickly. As you climb more, you will find preferences, maybe a different hitch, a mechanical device or a lighter rope, and you can swap parts as long as each new component is compatible.
Kits are also a good way to stock a backup set on the truck, so a damaged rope or device does not end the day.

Some climbers buy a kit as a starting point and keep the parts that work for them, then replace the rest over time. That is a perfectly good way to learn what you like without buying every option on its own.

If a kit does not include a saddle, choose one separately based on fit. If it does include one, check sizing carefully. A poorly fitting saddle is the one thing in a kit that is hard to live with, so make sure you can adjust or exchange it.
Sizing for helmets and lanyards matters too. A helmet should fit snugly with the chinstrap adjusted, and a lanyard should be long enough to wrap the stems you climb.
Hang in the saddle with the rest of the kit attached to check that everything sits where you expect it.

A kit is only as safe as the person climbing on it. Get hands-on training from a qualified instructor, read every component's instructions, and inspect your gear before every climb. All life-support components should meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's ratings for your use.
Keep the instruction sheets that come with each component in your gear bag or a binder on the truck. They contain the approved configurations and inspection criteria for each device.
Plan regular practice of aerial rescue with the kit, too. Knowing your own system well is part of being able to help a climber in trouble.

faq.q: Are tree climbing kits good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. A kit gives you a matched, compatible system, which is ideal when you are learning, as long as you also get proper training.

faq.q: Do climbing kits include a saddle?
faq.a: Some do and some do not. Check the contents list before you buy.

faq.q: Can I upgrade parts in a kit later?
faq.a: Yes, as long as each new part is compatible with your rope and the rest of the system.

name: Clothing
title: Arborist Clothing: Pants, Boots, Hats & Hoodies
meta: Arborist clothing and apparel for tree work: climbing pants, chainsaw pants, arborist boots, hats, hoodies and shirts built for climbing and cutting.
intro: Arborist clothing has to stretch for climbing, shed sawdust and sap, and stand up to brush and bark every day. Shop climbing pants, chainsaw pants, arborist boots, hats, hoodies and shirts built for tree work.

p: Tree work covers a lot of ground. A climber needs pants that move with the leg and resist abrasion, plus boots that work with spurs or on rope. Ground crew need cut protection when running a saw, and everyone needs visibility near traffic and layers for cold mornings. Good arborist apparel is built around these jobs instead of looking like it.

Cotton work clothes still have a place, but technical fabrics with stretch panels and reinforced knees last longer and are more comfortable in the tree. Brands like Arborwear, Arbortec and Clogger build clothing specifically for tree crews.
Gloves are part of the outfit too. Climbers often prefer thin, grippy gloves for rope work, while ground crew want heavier gloves for brush hauling and chipper feeding.

Arborist shirts work best with a fitted cut that does not snag on limbs or rope, and long sleeves give protection from sun, sap and scratches. Forestry clothing for logging and land clearing tends to be heavier, built for brush and cold, while climbing apparel leans lighter and stretchier.

Chainsaw pants and chaps contain fibers designed to clog the saw's sprocket when cut, stopping the chain before it reaches your leg. In the US, look for labels showing compliance with ASTM F1897 for leg protection, and for chainsaw boots, ASTM F1818. Many climbers wear chainsaw-protective pants aloft as well as on the ground.
No cut protection is cut proof. It works alongside training, good technique and a well-maintained saw.

Chainsaw-protective clothing should be replaced after it has been cut into the protective layer. Patching protective pants or chaps is generally not recommended unless the manufacturer allows it. Wash them according to the label, since harsh detergents and high heat can reduce effectiveness.

Arborist boots range from lightweight climbing boots to full chainsaw-protective boots. Hats and caps keep sun and sawdust off and add warmth under a helmet in winter, while hoodies and sweatshirts layer well for cold starts. Choose layers you can shed as the day warms up, and keep loose cords and drawstrings away from the saw.

Weather sets the layering plan. In summer, look for lightweight, breathable fabrics that dry fast and protect from sun. In winter, a base layer, an insulating hoodie and a windproof jacket give you a range to work with. Rain gear should be tough enough to survive brush.
Logging apparel such as heavy canvas can work for ground crews on cold days, but it is often too stiff for climbing.

High-visibility colors help the ground crew and drivers see you. When working near traffic, follow the applicable traffic control rules for your site. Always pair clothing with the rest of your protective equipment: helmet, eye and hearing protection and gloves.
When choosing clothing for a crew, consider buying in a common color so crew members are easy to spot and recognize on the site.

faq.q: What should arborists wear?
faq.a: Stretchy, durable pants or chainsaw-protective pants, supportive boots, layers for the weather, high visibility when needed, plus a helmet, eye and ear protection and gloves.

faq.q: Do climbers need chainsaw pants?
faq.a: Many climbers wear them whenever they run a saw. Requirements vary by employer and task, so follow your company's safety policy and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What is the best arborist clothing brand?
faq.a: Arborwear, Arbortec and Clogger are all popular with tree crews. The best choice depends on fit and the work you do.

faq.q: Is cotton okay for tree work?
faq.a: It works, but technical fabrics with stretch and reinforcement usually last longer and move better when climbing.

name: Arborist Boots
title: Tree Climbing Boots & Arborist Chainsaw Boots
meta: Tree climbing boots and arborist chainsaw boots from Arbortec and Arbpro. Supportive boots for spurs, rope work and ground saw work, with fit tips.
intro: Tree climbing boots have to support your arches on spurs, grip on rope and bark, and protect your feet around saws. Compare arborist boots from Arbortec and Arbpro, including chainsaw-protective models.

guide.h: What makes a good climbing boot
p: The best tree climbing boots combine a stiff shank, firm ankle support and a sole that grips. A stiff shank keeps the spur stirrup from crushing your arch and spreads load across the foot. Ankle support keeps you stable when you stand sideways on a stem. A sole with a defined heel helps foot ascenders and footlocking, and an aggressive tread grips wet bark and slopes.
Weight matters too. A lighter boot is easier on your legs over a long day of climbing. That is why many arborist climbing boots use lightweight materials while keeping the support where it counts.

Arborist boots often have extra features like reinforced toe caps that resist rope and bark wear, and hooks or loops that keep laces from snagging on spurs. Some arbpro boots use a clip and step system that makes lacing faster and keeps it secure.

Tree boots for climbing on rope only can be lighter and more flexible, but if you ever wear spurs, the stiff shank becomes essential. Many climbers own two pairs: a lighter boot for rope work and a supportive, stiff boot for spur work and removals. Matching boots to the day's work keeps your feet comfortable and stable.

Chainsaw boots include cut-protective layers in the upper that clog a running chain. In the US, chainsaw-protective footwear is covered by ASTM F1818; in Europe, by the EN ISO 17249 standard with protection classes. Check the label for what each boot is certified to. For ground crew bucking and felling, and climbers who run a saw a lot, cut-protective boots add a layer of protection on top of training and good technique.
Steel or composite toe caps are common in arborist boots too. Check whether the toe and cut protection suit your work and any requirements from your employer.

The Arbortec Scafell Lite is a lightweight chainsaw boot built for climbers who want protection without heavy weight. Arbpro models like the Andrew Cervino and the Clip N Step focus on support and fit for climbing and ground work. Consider your mix of work: mostly climbing, mostly ground saw work, or a mix. Waterproof membranes help in wet climates but can be warmer in summer.

Fit tree boots in the afternoon when your feet are slightly swollen, with the socks you work in. Your heel should not lift, toes should have room, and the boot should feel secure laced. Break new boots in on the ground before a long climb on spurs. Arborist boots with lace-lock or quick-lace systems save time and stay tight.

Clean off mud and sap, dry boots away from direct heat, and treat leather regularly. Replace boots when the shank softens, the sole wears smooth or any cut protection is damaged, because a cut-protective boot that has stopped a chain should be retired.
Replace laces as soon as they fray. A lace that snaps while you are on spurs is more than an inconvenience.

faq.q: What are the best tree climbing boots?
faq.a: Boots with a stiff shank, strong ankle support, a grippy sole and a defined heel, sized well for your feet. Chainsaw protection is a plus for climbers who run saws.

faq.q: Do I need chainsaw boots as a climber?
faq.a: Many climbers choose them. Requirements vary by employer and task, so follow your company policy and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Can I use regular work boots with spurs?
faq.a: Boots without a stiff shank let the spur stirrup press into your arch. Climbing-specific boots are far more comfortable and stable.

faq.q: How long do arborist boots last?
faq.a: It depends on use, but replace them when the shank softens, soles wear out or cut protection is damaged.

name: Hats & Caps
title: Tree Hats, Caps & Neck Warmers for Arborists
meta: Tree hats and caps for arborists: stocking caps, neck warmers and work hats from Arborwear and Husqvarna that fit under a helmet or wear on breaks.
intro: Tree hats and caps keep sun, sawdust and cold off your head on and off the job. We carry Arborwear stocking caps and neck warmers plus Husqvarna hats.

p: On the job, most of your time is under a helmet, so a hat needs to fit underneath it without changing how the helmet sits. A thin stocking cap or beanie adds warmth on cold mornings. A neck warmer keeps wind and sawdust out of your collar and can be pulled up over your face in bitter weather.
Off the helmet, a work hat with a brim keeps the sun off during brush hauling or chipper work. Many arborists also wear a tree logo hat as everyday crew gear.
Arborwear stocking caps and neck warmers are built for tree work with fabrics that hold up to bark and sawdust. Husqvarna hats are a good everyday option for the crew.
Look for flat seams and low-profile designs that will not create pressure points under the helmet suspension.

Before you wear any hat under a helmet, adjust the helmet so it still fits snug and the chinstrap sits correctly. A bulky hat can loosen the fit and reduce protection. Choose thin, close-fitting materials and readjust the helmet when you take the hat off later in the day.
Some climbing helmets have winter liners designed for them. These are a good alternative to a separate hat, because they are designed not to affect the helmet's fit.

Take your helmet to try-ons where you can, or test any new hat at home under the helmet before wearing it on the job. If the helmet will not adjust snug over the hat, the hat is too thick for climbing.

In winter, layering a thin cap with a neck warmer works better than one thick hat. Wool and synthetic blends stay warm when damp from sweat. Wash hats regularly, since sawdust and sweat break down fabric over time.
Keep loose cords and pom-poms away from saws and rope. Anything that can catch is a hazard in the tree.
Sun protection is easy to overlook in summer. A brimmed hat during ground work, sunscreen and a neck covering help prevent sunburn on long days in the open.
A spare dry cap in the truck is a small thing that makes a big difference on wet winter days.

Many tree companies outfit their crew with matching hats and caps. A consistent look helps customers recognize your crew on site and adds a professional touch. Choose durable styles that hold up to daily wear, and remember to keep logos and colors visible but not distracting near traffic.
Off the job, a tree hat is also a simple way to show what you do. The same rules apply: pick something comfortable and tough enough to survive the truck cab.
Btr tree hats and tree logo hats are popular searches for crew wear; whichever brand you choose, pick quality fabric and stitching that last.

faq.q: Can I wear a hat under my climbing helmet?
faq.a: Yes, if it is thin and the helmet still fits snugly with the chinstrap correctly adjusted.

faq.q: What hat is best for cold weather tree work?
faq.a: A thin wool or synthetic stocking cap under your helmet plus a neck warmer works well for most climbers.

faq.q: Do tree hats come in hi-vis colors?
faq.a: Some do. Bright colors help ground crew and drivers see you near the work area.

name: Sweatshirts & Jackets
title: Climbing Hoodies & Arborist Sweatshirts
meta: Climbing hoodies and arborist sweatshirts from Arborwear: double-thick hooded sweatshirts and hi-vis pullovers built for cold days of tree work.
intro: A good climbing hoodie or work sweatshirt is the layer you live in from fall through spring. We carry Arborwear double-thick hooded sweatshirts and safety yellow pullovers built for tree work.

guide.h: What makes a work hoodie last
p: Tree work wrecks regular sweatshirts fast. Look for heavier fabric, reinforced seams and cuffs that hold their shape. Double-thick construction blocks wind and holds up to bark and brush. A hoodie should allow full arm movement for climbing and cutting without riding up your back.
Fit matters with a saddle. A sweatshirt that is too long bunches under the waist belt, while one that is too short leaves your back exposed when you reach.

Arborwear double-thick hooded sweatshirts are made with two layers of fabric for warmth and durability, and they come in colors like black and navy that hide sap and dirt. Look for kangaroo pockets that keep small items close but do not snag.

A climbing hoodie also has to work under a helmet. A hood that is too bulky pushes the helmet forward or gets in the way of the chinstrap, so many climbers wear the hood down while climbing and pull it up only during breaks. Pick a hood with a shape that lies flat when not in use.

Hi-vis pullovers in safety yellow help drivers and ground crew see you near traffic or in a busy drop zone. Follow your site's rules for visibility. Keep hood drawstrings tucked away from saws, chippers and rope, and consider removing them entirely if they get in the way.
High-visibility colors are especially useful during storm work and short winter days when light is low.
If you work near chippers, keep sleeves snug at the wrist and avoid anything loose that could be pulled into the feed.

Cold mornings call for a base layer, a hoodie and a jacket you can shed as you warm up. Choose layers that are easy to take off and stash in the truck. Many climbers find a fitted sweatshirt better than a bulky jacket in the tree because it moves with them and does not snag.
Wash sweatshirts regularly to get sawdust and sap out of the fabric so they keep their warmth and last longer.

Landscaping hoodies and woodworking hoodies cover similar ground, but tree work is harder on fabric than most trades, so heavier construction pays off. Keep a spare hoodie in the truck for when the first one gets soaked.

When the weather turns wet or windy, a jacket over your hoodie keeps you working longer. Look for tough outer fabrics that survive brush, a cut that allows arm movement under a saddle, and cuffs that close around gloves. Avoid long, loose jackets that can catch on limbs, chippers or saws. In rain, a breathable waterproof jacket keeps you dry without trapping too much sweat.
For climbers, layering under a jacket can be tricky. Many prefer a fitted sweatshirt and a light shell rather than a heavy coat.

faq.q: Is a hoodie safe to wear while climbing?
faq.a: Yes, if it fits well and the hood and drawstrings are kept clear of rope, saws and chippers.

faq.q: Do you carry hi-vis sweatshirts?
faq.a: Yes, we carry safety yellow pullovers for crews working near traffic or in busy work zones.

faq.q: What size sweatshirt should I get for climbing?
faq.a: Pick a size that allows full arm movement without bunching under your saddle belt.

name: Climbing Pants
title: Arborist Trousers & Tree Climbing Pants
meta: Arborist trousers and tree climbing pants: Arborwear Ascender pants, Clogger chainsaw pants and Arbortec suspenders. Stretch and cut protection.
intro: Arborist trousers have to stretch for climbing, survive bark and brush, and in many cases stop a running chain. Shop tree climbing pants, chainsaw pants and suspenders.

p: Climbing pants like the Arborwear Ascender focus on stretch, durability and comfort under a saddle. They resist abrasion from bark and rope and move freely when you step high or footlock. They do not stop a chainsaw.

Arborist chainsaw pants, such as the Clogger Zero, contain layers of long fibers that pull out and jam the saw's sprocket when cut. In the US, look for a label showing compliance with ASTM F1897. Many climbers wear chainsaw pants aloft, and ground crew should wear chainsaw protection whenever they run a saw.

Look for pants labeled for protection from the front of the leg, or all-around protection if you need it. Climbing chainsaw pants often have stretch panels behind the leg so you can climb comfortably.
Remember that protection only works where it covers. Chainsaw pants protect the areas marked on the label; know where those zones are.

Look for a gusseted crotch and articulated knees so you can climb without the pants binding. Reinforced knees and cuffs last longer. Make sure the waist sits comfortably under your saddle belt without bunching. Chainsaw pants can be heavier, so suspenders help keep them up and take pressure off the waist.
Tree pants come in different weights for summer and winter work. Ventilation zips are a plus in hot weather.

Lumberjack pants and forest pants are other common names for durable work pants. Arborwear Ascender pants are a popular choice with climbers for their stretch and durability. Clogger Zero pants combine chainsaw protection with a lighter feel. Arbortec heavy-duty suspenders are made to hold up protective pants.

Tree pants with a stretch fabric that dries quickly are more comfortable on long days, and they are easier to clean when sap and sawdust stick to them. Large thigh pockets with closures keep phones and small tools secure when you are upside down.

Follow the washing instructions on the label, since harsh washing can reduce the effectiveness of protective fibers. Retire chainsaw pants that have been cut into the protective layer, or patch them only as the maker allows. Inspect them before each job for tears and worn spots.
Keep a spare pair of work pants in the truck. A tear high in the tree or a wet morning can make for a long day without a backup.
Pants work as part of a system with chainsaw boots, gloves, eye and ear protection and a helmet. No pants are cut proof. Training, technique and a well-maintained saw are the first line of defense.
If you prefer, chainsaw chaps worn over regular work pants are another option for ground work. Chaps are easy to put on and take off, but many climbers find pants more comfortable aloft.
Take time to fit pants with your saddle on, since a pair that feels fine standing may bind when you sit in the harness.

faq.q: Do tree climbing pants protect against chainsaws?
faq.a: Standard climbing pants do not. Only chainsaw-protective pants with cut-resistant layers are designed to stop a running chain.

faq.q: What are the best arborist trousers?
faq.a: Pants with stretch, reinforced knees and a good fit under your saddle. Choose chainsaw-protective pants if you run a saw.

faq.q: Can I wear chainsaw pants while climbing?
faq.a: Yes. Many climbers do, and climbing-specific chainsaw pants are designed for it.

faq.q: Why use suspenders with chainsaw pants?
faq.a: Chainsaw pants are heavier than regular pants, and suspenders keep them up without squeezing your waist under a saddle.

name: Cutting & Pruning
title: Tree Pruner, Hand Saw & Pole Saw Guide
meta: Tree pruner and pruning saw guide: hand saws, pole saws, pole pruners, poles, blades and hand pruners from Silky, Jameson, Marvin and Felco.
intro: Pick the right tree pruner, hand saw or pole saw and the work goes faster with cleaner cuts. This department covers Silky hand saws, Jameson and Marvin pole tools, Felco hand pruners, poles and replacement blades.

guide.h: Hand tools still do most of the pruning
p: Even on crews with a full lineup of chainsaws, much of the finest pruning work is done with hand tools. A sharp pull saw makes a clean cut with good control, without the noise or the extra hazard of a running saw. Hand saws are also lighter to carry in the tree and quick to use on small to mid-size limbs.
From the ground, pole saws and pole pruners let you reach deadwood, clear sidewalks and lift crowns without climbing. A good pole setup handles a lot of small-tree and street-tree work by itself.

Silky saws have a strong following among climbers for their sharp, fast-cutting blades. Felco hand pruners are known for durability and replaceable parts. Jameson and Marvin build pole tools that hold up to daily crew use.

guide.h: Hand saws, pole saws and pruners
p: Hand saws come in straight and curved blades. Curved blades cut aggressively on the pull and suit overhead cuts, while straight blades give more control for precise cuts. A scabbard on your saddle or belt keeps the saw ready and protects you from the teeth.

Pole saws pair a saw head with fiberglass or aluminum poles, and pole pruners add a cutting head with a rope-pulled blade for small limbs. Bypass hand pruners handle the smallest cuts. Each tool in this department has its own section and buying guide.
Replacement blades keep favorite saws in service, and scabbards protect both the blade and the person carrying it. Poles come in sections that build to the length you need.

guide.h: Good pruning starts with good cuts
p: The ANSI A300 standard describes how to make proper pruning cuts: cut outside the branch collar, avoid leaving stubs, and use the three-cut method on heavier limbs to prevent bark tearing. Sharp tools make this much easier. A dull saw tears wood and encourages rushed cuts.

Use the right tool for the size of the cut. A hand pruner for twigs, a hand saw for small and medium limbs, and a chainsaw only when the cut calls for it. Forcing a small tool through a large cut leads to tearing and poor results.

Clean cuts also save time. A clean, well-placed cut rarely needs to be redone, and a tree that is pruned well needs less correction work later. That is better for the tree and for your client relationships.

Never use conductive poles near energized lines, and only qualified line-clearance arborists should work within the minimum approach distances to power lines. Fiberglass poles rated for electrical work are used for line clearance, but they still require training, inspection and the correct procedures under ANSI Z133.
Keep blades sheathed when moving around the site, wear eye protection and gloves when cutting, and keep the drop zone clear for the ground crew.
Wipe and dry all cutting tools at the end of the day.

faq.q: What is the best tree pruner for small limbs?
faq.a: A sharp bypass hand pruner for the smallest cuts, then a pull saw or pole pruner as limbs get thicker or higher.

faq.q: Curved or straight hand saw?
faq.a: Curved blades cut fast, especially overhead. Straight blades give more control for precise cuts. Many climbers carry one of each.

faq.q: Can I use a pole saw near power lines?
faq.a: Only qualified line-clearance workers should prune near energized lines, using properly rated insulated tools and following ANSI Z133.

faq.q: How do I keep pruning saw blades sharp?
faq.a: Most modern pull saws use hardened teeth that are not resharpened. Replace the blade when it dulls or bends.

name: Replacement Blades
title: Replacement Pruning Saw Blades
meta: Replacement pruning saw blades for arborist hand saws and pole saws, including the Notch 13 inch tri-edge blade and the Silky Sugoi replacement blade.
intro: Fresh pruning saw blades bring a tired saw back to full speed. We carry replacement blades like the Notch 13 inch tri-edge and the Silky Sugoi blade.

p: Most modern pruning saws use impulse-hardened teeth that are very sharp but are not meant to be resharpened. When cuts slow down, the blade binds, or teeth are chipped or bent, swap in a new blade. Match the replacement to your saw model and mounting style, tighten it correctly, and check it before every use. Wear gloves when changing blades.

Replacement blades are specific to each saw. The Silky Sugoi replacement blade fits the Sugoi frame, while the Notch 13 inch tri-edge saw blade fits compatible pole saw heads and handles. Tri-edge teeth cut on the pull stroke and clear chips fast. Check blade length, tooth style and the mounting pattern before buying. Keep a spare blade in the truck so a broken blade does not end the day.
Store spare blades in a sheath or the original packaging so the teeth stay sharp and nobody gets cut digging through the tool box. Wipe sap off with a solvent safe for the blade's coating.

faq.q: Can I sharpen my pruning saw blade?
faq.a: Most hardened-tooth pull saw blades are not designed to be resharpened. Replace them when they dull.

name: Hand Saws & Scabbards
title: Arborist Hand Saws & Scabbards: Silky Saws
meta: Arborist hand saws and scabbards from Silky: the Zubat, Sugoi, Gomtaro and Gunfighter. Curved and straight pull saws with sheaths for climbers.
intro: An arborist hand saw is the tool you reach for on almost every climb. We carry Silky pull saws including the Zubat, Sugoi, Gomtaro and Gunfighter, each with a scabbard to carry it on your saddle or belt.

p: A curved hand saw bites hard on the pull stroke, which makes it fast for overhead cuts and larger limbs. A straight blade gives better control and a cleaner finish for precise pruning cuts. Many climbers carry a curved saw on one side of the saddle and a smaller straight saw on the other.

Length matters too. A saw with a long blade cuts larger limbs quickly but is heavier and harder to handle in tight spots. Saws around 300 to 330 mm, like the Gomtaro 300 and Gunfighter 330, are a popular middle ground.

The Silky Zubat is a classic curved arborist saw with an aggressive tooth pattern. The Sugoi is a large curved saw for fast cutting. The Gomtaro is a straight saw known for being tough and reliable, and it is also popular for cutting roots. The Gunfighter is designed with arborists in mind, with a scabbard built for carrying on a saddle.
A curved hand saw with a long blade is the go-to choice for many removal climbers, while pruning specialists often prefer a shorter straight blade.

A hand saw with a sheath is safer to carry and easier to reach. Most Silky saws come with a scabbard that clips to your saddle or belt. Mount it where you can draw and return the saw with one hand without looking, and check that the retention holds the saw securely when you are upside down in the tree.
Many climbers tether their hand saw so it cannot fall into the drop zone.
A tether can be as simple as a short cord between the saw handle and a saddle loop. Make sure it is long enough to make full strokes but short enough not to tangle with your climbing system.

Pull saws cut on the pull stroke, so let the saw do the work and avoid forcing it on the push. Use the three-cut method on heavier limbs to prevent bark tearing, and make final cuts just outside the branch collar, as described in ANSI A300. Keep your free hand well away from the blade path.
When working aloft, position yourself so you are not reaching across your body or cutting toward your own rope or lanyard. A sharp saw cuts rope as easily as wood.

Wipe sap off the blade after use and keep it dry to prevent rust. Most hardened-tooth blades are not resharpened; replace the blade when it dulls or bends. Replacement blades are available for many Silky models in our blades section.
Keep your hand saw scabbard clean too. Sawdust and sap build up inside and can make the saw stick, which is frustrating and unsafe when you need to draw it quickly.
Rust on a blade slows cuts and weakens teeth. A light coat of oil after cleaning helps in wet weather, but wipe off excess before use so it does not pick up grit.

faq.q: What is the best arborist hand saw?
faq.a: It depends on your work. Curved saws like the Zubat cut fast overhead, while straight saws give more control. Silky saws are a long-time favorite of climbers.

faq.q: Do Silky saws come with a scabbard?
faq.a: Most models do. Check the product listing for what is included.

faq.q: Can I replace the blade on a Silky saw?
faq.a: Yes, replacement blades are available for many Silky models.

name: Pole Saws & Scabbards
h1: Pruning Saw on a Pole: Pole Saws & Heads
title: Pole Saws: Pruning Saw on a Pole & Saw Heads
meta: Pole saws for arborists: a pruning saw on a pole with telescoping aluminum poles, Jameson pole saw kits and Marvin cast saw heads, plus blade advice.
intro: A pruning saw on a pole lets you reach deadwood and clearance cuts from the ground. We carry telescoping pole saws, Jameson pruner and pole saw kits, and Marvin cast saw heads.

p: Telescoping pole saws are compact and quick to adjust, while sectional poles with a separate saw head are tougher and easier to repair. Pick a saw blade length that suits the size of the limbs you cut, and make sure the head fits your pole system. Fiberglass poles are needed for work near power, but only qualified line-clearance workers should be near energized lines. Wear a helmet and eye protection and stay out from under the cut.

A cast saw head, like the Marvin, mounts a pruning saw blade on the end of a pole. Saw blades for pole saws come in different lengths and tooth patterns. A pole saw scabbard protects the blade during transport and keeps the crew safe from the teeth. The Jameson LS kit combines a pruner, a pole saw and poles in one package. A telescoping aluminum pole saw like the Nobasu is light and compact, but aluminum is conductive and must not be used near power.

faq.q: What is a pole saw used for?
faq.a: Pruning limbs out of reach from the ground, such as deadwood removal, crown raising and sidewalk clearance.

name: Poles & Kits
title: Tree Pole Sections & Pruner Pole Kits
meta: Tree pole sections and pruner pole kits: Jameson fiberglass poles, foam-filled poles and ash peavey poles for pole saws, pruners and tree work.
intro: A good tree pole system is the backbone of pruning from the ground. Mix and match fiberglass sections, foam-filled poles and kits to reach the cuts you need.

p: Fiberglass poles are the standard for pole saws and pole pruners because they are strong, light and resist conducting electricity when clean and dry. Hollow-core poles are lighter; foam-filled poles keep moisture from collecting inside, which helps preserve their dielectric properties. Wooden poles, such as ash, are still used for tools like peaveys, where toughness matters more than weight.
Foam-filled fiberglass poles are the usual pick for crews that do any work near utilities, but remember that only qualified line-clearance workers should be near energized lines.

Long pole saws for trees are typically built from multiple fiberglass sections, so choosing the right tree pole system early saves money and frustration later. Pick one system and stick with it so all sections and heads interchange.

Sectional poles connect end to end, so you can carry a few short sections and assemble the length you need. Most systems use a snap-button or locking connection. Keep sections from the same system together and check that each connection seats fully.

A pole pruner uses a rope to pull a cutting blade through small limbs. Keep the pole saw rope in good shape and routed so it cannot snag. A stiff, straight pole makes the work much easier at full length.
Rope poles and robel poles show up in searches too. Whatever you call them, the key is a strong, straight, well-maintained pole that fits your heads.

Wipe poles clean after use, store them dry and off the ground, and inspect for cracks, splinters and damaged ends before each job. A cracked fiberglass pole can fail under load and may not be safe near power. Retire damaged sections.
Wear a helmet and eye protection when working with poles, and keep the ground crew out of the drop zone.

Clean fiberglass poles with a mild cleaner made for the purpose and keep the surface free of deep scratches. Some crews apply a silicone or wax finish to help shed moisture, following the pole maker's advice. Damaged gel coat lets moisture into the fiberglass, which is a concern for any work near power.

A pole kit gives you sections, a saw head and a pruner head that work together, which is a good way to start a pole system. Add sections over time as you need more reach. Jameson poles are widely used in the trade, and their 8 foot hollow-core poles are a common choice. Six foot foam-filled poles are easier to carry and store. A peavey with a 12 foot ash pole is a different kind of tool, used for rolling and moving logs.
When tying a rope to a pole, such as for a pruner, follow the manufacturer's instructions for routing and attaching the rope.
Store pole sections in a rack or tube on the truck to keep them from bouncing around and cracking. Keep heads sheathed during transport.

faq.q: Are fiberglass tree poles safe near power lines?
faq.a: Clean, dry, properly maintained fiberglass poles resist conduction, but only qualified line-clearance workers should be near energized lines, following ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What is the advantage of foam-filled poles?
faq.a: Foam keeps moisture and contaminants from building up inside the pole, which helps maintain its insulating properties.

faq.q: How long should my pole system be?
faq.a: Carry enough sections to reach your usual cuts. Many crews build to around 12 to 18 feet for routine pruning.

title: Tree Pruners: Felco Hand Pruners & Marvin Heads
meta: Tree pruners for arborists: Felco 2 hand pruners and Marvin pole pruner heads for clean cuts on small limbs, from the ground or up in the tree.
intro: Tree pruners make the smallest, cleanest cuts. We carry the Felco 2 hand pruner and Marvin pole pruner heads for cutting small limbs from the ground.

guide.h: Hand pruners and pole pruner heads
p: A bypass hand pruner like the Felco 2 handles small live twigs and branches with a clean scissor cut. For small limbs out of reach, a pole pruner head on a fiberglass pole uses a rope-driven blade to snip from the ground. Keep blades sharp and adjusted, oil the pivot, and replace worn blades. Wear eye protection and keep your free hand out of the cut.

The Felco 2 is a classic bypass hand pruner with replaceable blades and parts. The Marvin pruner head and bull pruner head with single pulley mount on fiberglass poles for pruning from the ground. The bull pruner head handles slightly larger limbs. Look at cutting capacity, how the blade is driven and whether the head fits your poles. Clean sap off blades after use and keep them sharp for clean cuts that heal well.
Replacement blades and springs are available for many of these tools.

faq.q: What size cuts can a pole pruner make?
faq.a: Pole pruners are for small limbs. Check the head's maximum cutting capacity and use a pole saw for anything larger.

name: Jobsite
title: Arborist Jobsite Gear: Bucket Truck & Site Safety
meta: Arborist jobsite gear for tree crews: bucket truck and aerial lift accessories, fall protection, scabbards, outrigger pads and site safety equipment.
intro: Arborist jobsite gear covers everything around the tree that keeps the work moving and the crew safe: bucket truck accessories, aerial lift fall protection, outrigger pads, chocks and site safety equipment.

p: Climbing gear gets most of the attention, but a good jobsite runs on the gear around it. Wheel chocks and outrigger pads keep trucks and lifts stable. Bucket covers and scabbards protect equipment and tools. Fall protection keeps operators in aerial lifts connected. Each of these pieces prevents a specific problem that crews run into every week.
Organizing jobsite gear on the truck matters too. When chocks, cones, pads and first aid have a set place, setup and teardown go faster and nothing is left at the last job.

Rigging gear, chippers and stump grinders are their own topics, but the support gear around them matters just as much. Think about what slows your crew down or creates risk on a typical day, and buy gear that fixes those problems.
A wheel chock is the simplest piece of jobsite gear, and also one of the most important. Make chocking the truck the first step on every stop.

Aerial lifts are a major part of tree work, especially for utility and municipal crews. Operators need a full body harness and a lanyard attached to the manufacturer's designated anchor point, plus tools that store safely in the bucket. Our bucket truck and aerial lift section covers harnesses, lanyards, scabbards and bucket accessories.
Follow the lift manufacturer's operating instructions, the applicable ANSI A92 standards and ANSI Z133 for tree work from aerial devices.

Bucket truck work brings its own hazards: overhead power lines, unstable ground and traffic. The right accessories and a disciplined setup routine help manage all three. Plan where the truck will sit, check overhead clearances and keep minimum approach distances from energized lines.

Before work starts, a jobsite briefing should cover the work plan, hazards, drop zones, communication and emergency procedures. Set up traffic control where the work affects roads or sidewalks, following the applicable rules. Chock trucks, deploy outrigger pads on soft ground, and keep the chipper area clear.
Make sure the crew has first aid supplies and knows how to perform an aerial rescue if someone is climbing.
Fire extinguishers on every truck and chipper, plus eyewash where needed, round out a basic jobsite kit. Check them regularly and replace used or expired items.

Look for gear that is built for daily use in rough conditions: composite outrigger pads that will not rot, chocks that suit your vehicle's tire size, covers that fit your bucket. Buying for the specific equipment on your trucks saves money and frustration.

Consistency helps on multi-truck crews. When every truck carries the same chocks, pads, cones and first aid kit, any crew member can set up any truck without hunting for gear. Make a checklist for each truck and review it regularly. Replace worn or damaged items before they become a problem.

faq.q: What jobsite gear does a tree crew need?
faq.a: At minimum: wheel chocks, cones or traffic control gear, a first aid kit, fire extinguisher and appropriate fall protection and accessories for any aerial lift.

faq.q: Do I need outrigger pads?
faq.a: On soft ground, asphalt or turf, outrigger pads spread the load and help keep the truck stable and protect the surface.

faq.q: What fall protection is required in a bucket truck?
faq.a: Generally a full body harness with a lanyard attached to the lift's designated anchor. Follow the manufacturer, ANSI A92 and your employer's policy.

faq.q: Where can I find bucket truck accessories?
faq.a: In our bucket truck and aerial lift gear section, including covers, scabbards and outrigger pads.

name: Bucket Truck & Lift Gear
h1: Bucket Truck Harness & Aerial Lift Gear
title: Bucket Truck Harness & Aerial Lift Gear
meta: Bucket truck harness, lanyard and aerial lift gear for tree crews: fall arrest, scabbards, bucket covers and outrigger pads for safe lift work.
intro: From the bucket truck harness to tool scabbards and outrigger pads, this section has the gear tree crews use when working from aerial lifts.

p: A bucket truck safety harness is a full body harness designed for fall arrest, worn with a lanyard attached to the lift's designated anchor point. Pair it with a shock-absorbing or self-retracting lanyard of an appropriate length, scabbards that keep tools organized in the bucket, and accessories like covers and outrigger pads. Follow the lift manufacturer's instructions, ANSI A92, ANSI Z133 and your employer's policy, and inspect harnesses and lanyards before every use.

Bucket truck and aerial lift scabbards hold hand saws, pole saws and pruners securely at the edge of the bucket so they are ready to grab and cannot fall. Bucket covers keep rain and debris out when the truck is parked. Outrigger pads and wheel chocks keep the truck stable. Keep the bucket uncluttered, and never use the bucket as a crane or tie-in point for rigging unless the manufacturer specifically allows it.
Inspect scabbards for cracks and worn retention.

faq.q: Can I use my climbing saddle in a bucket truck?
faq.a: A tree climbing saddle is a work positioning harness, not a fall arrest harness. Use a full body harness for aerial lift fall protection unless the lift and policy allow otherwise.

name: Bucket Truck Accessories
title: Bucket Truck Accessories: Covers, Pads & Chocks
meta: Bucket truck accessories for tree crews: two-man bucket covers, Bigfoot composite outrigger pads and wheel chocks that keep the truck stable and protected.
intro: The right bucket truck accessories protect your equipment and keep the truck stable on the job. We carry two-man bucket covers, composite outrigger pads and wheel chocks.

p: Wheel chocks should go in place every time the truck is parked for work. Outrigger pads spread the load on soft ground and protect pavement and turf; composite pads are light and will not rot like wood. A bucket cover keeps rain and debris out of the bucket between jobs, protecting the liner and controls. Choose accessories sized for your specific truck and bucket, and follow the lift manufacturer's setup instructions.

Two-man bucket covers, like the Weaver cover, are sized for larger buckets used on utility and tree trucks. Other bucket truck supplies include scabbards, tool holders and storage that keep the bucket organized. Bucket truck parts such as liners and controls should come from the manufacturer or an approved supplier. Check accessories regularly for wear, especially chocks and outrigger pads that see daily abuse.
Store chocks and pads where they are easy to grab so setting them out is quick and becomes a habit on every stop.

faq.q: Why use composite outrigger pads?
faq.a: They are strong, lighter than many alternatives and do not rot or split, so they last longer on a working truck.

name: Aerial Lift Fall Arrest
h1: Fall Protection Harness and Lanyard for Aerial Lifts
title: Fall Protection Harness and Lanyard for Lifts
meta: Fall protection harness and lanyard kits for bucket trucks, boom lifts and scissor lifts: Safewaze kits, retractable lanyards and the Petzl Absorbica.
intro: A fall protection harness and lanyard is required gear for most aerial lift work. We carry Safewaze fall protection kits, web retractable lanyards and the Petzl Absorbica energy-absorbing lanyard.

p: Aerial lift fall protection is a system. The full body harness distributes forces across your thighs, pelvis, chest and shoulders. The lanyard connects your harness's dorsal D-ring to the lift's designated anchor point. Energy absorbers or self-retracting lanyards limit the force on your body if you are ejected from the bucket or basket.

Body belts and tree climbing saddles are not fall arrest harnesses. For fall arrest on a boom lift harness setup or bucket harness, use a full body harness rated for that purpose, typically to ANSI Z359 requirements.
Fall protection is the last line of defense. Good lift operation, a stable setup and staying inside the platform come first.

guide.h: Boom lifts, bucket trucks and scissor lifts
p: On boom lifts and bucket trucks, the operator must be tied off to the anchor provided by the lift manufacturer. On scissor lifts, the guardrails are typically the primary protection, but many employers and lift manufacturers require a scissor lift harness and restraint lanyard too. Check your lift's manual and your company policy.

Lanyard length matters. Too long and you could be ejected and fall a long way before the lanyard catches. Many crews prefer a short lanyard or a restraint setup that keeps the operator inside the platform entirely.

Harnesses for bucket trucks often include features like a dorsal D-ring placement that works well in the bucket and padding for comfort over a full shift. Quick-connect leg and chest buckles make it easier to put the harness on correctly every time.

A fall protection kit bundles a harness and lanyard so you get a matched system. Check harness sizing, the lanyard's length and energy absorber, and the connector type for your lift's anchor. Retractable web lanyards stay taut and out of the way, which helps in a busy bucket.

The Safewaze economy fall protection kit is a simple way to equip a crew with a harness and lanyard. The six foot web retractable lanyard stays taut and reduces slack. The Petzl Absorbica-I is an energy-absorbing lanyard with a single connector, designed to limit forces in a fall. Choose components that are compatible with each other and with your lift.
Size harnesses for the operator who will wear them, and adjust straps every time a different person puts one on. A loose harness can cause serious injuries in a fall.

Inspect harnesses and lanyards before each use for cuts, abrasion, heat damage, deployed energy absorbers and damaged hardware. Remove from service any equipment that has arrested a fall. Every lift operator should be trained in lift operation and fall protection, and a rescue plan should be in place.
Cherry picker and boom lift operators should never untie while the platform is elevated. Plan the work so you can reach what you need without leaning over the rails.
Store harnesses and lanyards clean, dry and away from sunlight and chemicals. Hang them up rather than leaving them crumpled in the bucket, where they can be damaged by tools, saws and debris.

faq.q: Do I need a harness in a bucket truck?
faq.a: Yes. Operators in bucket trucks and boom lifts are generally required to wear a full body harness and lanyard attached to the designated anchor.

faq.q: Is a scissor lift harness required?
faq.a: Requirements vary. Guardrails are the main protection, but many employers and manufacturers require a harness and restraint lanyard. Check your lift manual and policy.

faq.q: Can I use my tree saddle for aerial lift fall protection?
faq.a: No. A tree climbing saddle is a work positioning harness. Use a full body fall arrest harness.

faq.q: How often should I replace my fall protection harness?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's guidance and retire it immediately after a fall or if inspection shows damage.
